sections.b: Move it back in ONE PIECE — hands, arms and chest turn together, no early wrist roll. FEET/KNEES: quiet; weight just starting to press into the trail heel. HIPS: barely rotating — the TRAIL hip is turning BEHIND you, not sliding out over the trail foot (that slide is a sway). CHECKPOINT: shaft parallel to the target line, toe pointing up, hands over the trail thigh, lead arm straight and still across the chest.
sections.k: One-piece takeaway: the trail hip turns BEHIND you, it doesn't slide out over the foot.

sections.t: 3 · Top of the backswing
sections.b: FEET: pressure loaded into the trail heel and instep; lead heel can stay down or lift slightly — either is fine. KNEES: the TRAIL knee HOLDS its address flex — if it straightens, you've swayed/stood up. HIPS: turned ~45° so your belt buckle points right of the ball, and you feel LOADED into the trail glute — like you're sitting into that right hip. Trail hip should still be inside the trail foot (outside it = sway). SPINE: same tilt you set at address, unchanged. SHOULDERS: turned ~90°, lead shoulder under the chin, upper back to the target — shoulders turn about twice as much as the hips (that gap is your coil). ARMS/HANDS: lead arm comfortably straight; TRAIL ELBOW points more DOWN at the ground and stays IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam (your working feel); shaft points at / parallel to the target line — not laid off across it. HEAD: still behind the ball, quiet.
sections.k: Trail knee holds its flex and hips turn ~45° — if the knee straightens, you've swayed.

sections.t: 4 · Transition — how the downswing STARTS (your problem spot)
sections.b: The ORDER is the whole game, and it runs ground-up WHILE the club is still finishing the backswing. (1) FEET/PRESSURE FIRST: press down into the LEAD foot — feel pressure move to the lead heel/instep. (2) HIPS SECOND: the LEAD hip then CLEARS — it rotates open (turns left) and back behind you and UP — while (3) the arms and club simply DROP into the slot (this is exactly your one-arm feel). You are NOT shoving the hips toward the target; you're turning them out of the way so the arms have room to fall. TRAIL SIDE: trail heel starts to lift, trail knee kicks in toward the lead knee. CHECKPOINT (down-the-line): when your hands reach hip height, the shaft should point at or just outside the ball and your hips are ALREADY opening. If the hands get to the ball before the hips have turned, you cast.
sections.k: Your problem spot. The order is ground-up: pressure into the lead foot, then hips, then chest, then arms.

sections.t: 5 · Impact — the position all of it is for
sections.b: FEET: ~80–90% of pressure on the LEAD foot; trail foot up on the inside of the toe. LEAD LEG: straightening / 'posting up' — this extension pulls the hips up and around and is a big chunk of the speed you lose when you slide instead. HIPS: OPEN ~35–45° to the target — belt buckle already pointing LEFT of the ball, lead hip HIGH and behind you. SPINE/CHEST: still tilted, chest 'covering' the ball; for irons and wedges you stay DOWN through it. HANDS: ahead of the ball for irons (shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh); level for driver so you catch it slightly on the up. HEAD: still behind the ball, eyes down. This is the money frame — most of the checkpoints above exist only to get you here.
sections.k: Impact is 80–90% on the lead foot with the lead leg posting up and the hips already open 35–45°.

sections.t: 6 · Follow-through & finish
sections.b: Keep rotating — the belt buckle turns from left-of-the-ball all the way to facing the target and past it. FEET: fully onto the lead foot, trail foot balanced on the toe with the laces to the target. HIPS: fully cleared and open, LEAD LEG tall and straight. CHEST: faces the target, then left of it. ARMS: extend down the line just after impact (the 'chase'), then fold up to a tall, balanced finish. Test: if you can HOLD the finish for 3 seconds without falling off balance, your sequence and weight shift were good.
sections.k: Keep rotating to a full, tall finish — the belt buckle ends past the target.

sections.t: 7 · The HIPS in plain terms — SLIDE vs CLEAR (read twice)
sections.b:
You're unsure here, so plainly: coming down, the hips can do two different things. A SLIDE is the hips moving SIDEWAYS toward the target — the belt buckle stays pointing at the ball, the hips stay 'closed,' and your upper body hangs back to counterbalance. That is the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' miss: no speed, hands flip to square the face, thin or fat strikes. A CLEAR (what you want) is the hips ROTATING — the lead hip turns back behind you and up as the lead leg straightens, so the belt buckle points LEFT of the ball at impact. THREE IMAGES that make it click: (a) There's a wall just behind your lead butt cheek — clearing = that cheek moves BACK to the wall, not toward the target. (b) You're standing in a barrel — you can TURN inside it but you can't slide out of it. (c) Pull your lead back pocket around behind you and up. Note: a SMALL lateral shift is real and necessary — but it happens in the FEET (pressure to the lead foot), and THEN the hips turn. Feet shift, hips spin — never the whole pelvis sliding as one block.

SINCE UPDATED — AUG 20 2026, AND READ THIS BEFORE YOU WORK ON IT. Everything above is still a correct description of what a slide and a clear ARE, which is what this checkpoint page is for. What is no longer true is the sentence calling the slide YOUR miss. The Aug 17 on-course driver film caught a finish for the first time — complete and balanced — and a swing whose hips genuinely stall cannot finish there. So the hips do clear, and the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' symptom is now read as LOSING POSTURE, i.e. height, not as a hip slide. The live diagnosis and the drills that earn their time are in SWING FOCUS — POSTURE & THE TOP. Keep this section as the definition; do not take it as the diagnosis.
sections.k: Read twice: a slide keeps the buckle at the ball, a clear turns it left around a post.

sections.t: 8 · How to groove it (feel beats positions)
sections.b: Positions are for the mirror; feels are for hitting. Best hip drills, all in your Swing Focus plan: TRAIL-FOOT-BACK step-through and LEAD-HIP-TO-THE-WALL — both make 'clear, don't slide' automatic because sliding is physically blocked. Then the ONE-HANDED Miracle 201 drop to feel the club fall while the hips open. Rehearse a checkpoint at ~50% speed until the shape is in; full speed returns on its own once the body trusts the position. One checkpoint at a time — stack them over weeks, not in one range session.
sections.k: Positions are for the mirror, feels are for hitting — groove it with the trail-foot-back and wall drills.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: What changed here and when.
sections.b: AUG 30 2026 — appended the Aug 20 correction to section 7. It was the last live carrier of the hips-stall diagnosis, which the posture plan retracted on Aug 20 off the first film to catch a finish; the old Swing Focus — Hips plan was retired then, but this section was never revisited, so two standing plans were making opposite claims about the same miss. The definition is kept and the diagnosis retracted, rather than rewriting the section, because it is a reference for what the positions mean.

rules: ONE checkpoint per session — not all nine
Ground-up order in transition: pressure → hips → chest → arms
CLEAR the hips around a post, never slide them at the target
Mirror for positions, drills for feels

briefing.note: Film date only. 'appended the Aug 20 correction' and 'retracted on Aug 20' are edit dates and stay.

briefing.course: The Grip — Before the Club Moves
briefing.focus:
The full-swing hold, and what you are actually after with it: TIGHTER COMPRESSION. Not a slice cure — you corrected that within the hour on Sep 9 — and not something the driver has any part in, because its weight is dialled and staying where it is.

Compression is the ball first, the ground after, with the shaft still leaning at the target. A stronger lead hand does not produce that by itself. What it does is remove the REASON to flip: with the hand rotated, the face is square with your lead wrist FLAT, so holding the lean stops costing you a shut face. That is a real mechanism and it is why the instinct is a good one — but it makes the strike AVAILABLE rather than delivering it, which is why the gate in this plan is the DIVOT and the FACE, never the ball flight.

Every section says SOURCE · YOURS or SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE, so you can see at a glance which lines are yours and which are somebody else's teaching.
rules: You are chasing COMPRESSION — ball first, ground after, shaft still leaning
Lead hand: 2.5–3 knuckles, V outside the trail shoulder
FINGERS, not the palm — the putting grip is the opposite hold, on purpose
Both hands MATCH: the trail V runs parallel to the lead V
The grip removes the reason to FLIP. It cannot move your low point
Judge it on the DIVOT and the face tape, never on how it felt
PHOTOGRAPH it before you move it, and one knuckle at a time
Driver weight stays put — it is your control, not a second lever
Starts left AND curves left? Too strong for your path — back it off

sections.t: WHAT YOU SAID, AND WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS
sections.k: Your description of a strong grip is textbook-accurate — the only line that needs a guard is the one calling it a slice fix.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, CHECKED AGAINST STANDARD PRACTICE.

WHAT YOU SAID (Sep 9 2026): you want a stronger left hand. Rotated further clockwise on the club, two and a half to three knuckles showing at address, the V between thumb and index finger pointing past your right shoulder toward the armpit or outside the shoulder, and the club sitting across the FINGERS rather than buried in the palm. You listed the trade yourself: it closes the face and reduces a slice, it releases without a wrist flip, it makes the club easier to get on plane — and it hooks if body rotation stalls or the grip goes too far.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS: the same thing, close to word for word. Knuckle count, V direction, fingers over palm and the hook risk are how every teacher describes a strong lead hand, and there is nothing eccentric in what you sent.

THE VERDICT IS THAT YOU ARE ON TRACK, and that is a real result rather than a polite one. You are not about to build something odd, and the rest of this plan can be about building it properly instead of about whether to build it.

WHERE IT NEEDS A GUARD, and it is one line out of the lot: 'fixes slices'. That is true of a slice caused by an open FACE. The fault open on your card is a PATH fault — over the top, out to in — and it is a different animal. That does not change the hold you build. It changes what to expect from it, and how you read the ball afterwards.

AND WHAT IT IS FOR, which you said next and which changes the emphasis of this whole plan: 'just looking to tighten up my compression with the grip mainly.' That is a better reason than the one the textbook leads with, and it is a different mechanism — the next section is the one to read. The slice material below stays, but as a GUARD on how far to take this rather than as the point of it.

sections.t: COMPRESSION — and the grip's actual share of it
sections.k: A grip cannot move your low point; what it removes is the REASON to flip, and the flip is what kills compression.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS for the goal, STANDARD PRACTICE for the mechanism.

WHAT COMPRESSION IS, in one line: the ball first, the ground after, with the shaft still leaning toward the target at impact. Everything else people mean by the word follows from that — the lower flight, the extra spin, the sound. The physical version: the low point of the arc sits PAST the ball, so the club is still descending when it arrives, and the dynamic loft is less than the loft stamped on the sole.

WHAT THE GRIP HAS TO DO WITH IT, and this is worth being precise about because it decides what to expect. A grip cannot move your low point. What it changes is what your LEAD WRIST has to do to square the face. With a weaker lead hand the face arrives open unless something rotates it, and the quickest thing available is the trail hand throwing past — a flip. A flip adds loft and throws the low point BEHIND the ball, which is the exact opposite of compression, and it is the most common reason a good player cannot compress an iron.

SO A STRONGER LEAD HAND REMOVES THE REASON TO FLIP. The face is square with the lead wrist flat, which means holding the shaft leaning forward no longer costs you a shut face. Your hands stop having to choose between squaring the face and keeping the lean. That is the real case for this change and it is a good one.

WHAT IT IS NOT is the mechanism itself. Compression is mostly low point and where your pressure is at impact, and a stronger grip with the same flip in it gives you a hook and no compression at all. The grip makes the strike AVAILABLE; your body still has to deliver it. Which is exactly why the gate in this plan is the divot and the face tape — a flight can flatter you, a divot cannot.

AND THE IMPACT NUMBERS ARE NOT MEASURED ON YOU. Swing film does exist — a Jul 19 simulator pair, driver and wedge stills from Jul 26, and the Aug 17 Lakeside driver clip those on-course stills were pulled from — and between them they give tempo (~3:1, Jul 19), a full coil, a lower-body transition and a held finish. What none of them has ever produced is a number AT IMPACT: your low point, your attack angle and your shaft lean are all still unknown, because every capture so far was either stills, a screen recording, or shot at 60 fps where the driver head moves about two and a half feet between frames. One face-on set at 240 fps closes the first two, and it is on the swing to-do.

sections.t: THE HOLD — build it the same way every time
sections.k: Lead hand across the fingers with the heel pad on top, then the trail hand MATCHES it; a strong lead and a neutral trail is two hands fighting.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE — textbook teaching, and nothing of yours has moved it.

LEAD HAND (left) first, with the club held out in front of you so gravity is not making the decision for you. The handle runs diagonally across the FINGERS — from the base of the index finger to just under the heel pad — and then you close the hand so the fleshy pad at the heel sits ON TOP of the handle. That pad on top is what a strong grip actually IS. The knuckles are how you check it, not the thing itself.

CHECK IT THREE WAYS, and all three should agree. TWO AND A HALF TO THREE KNUCKLES visible when you look down. The V between thumb and index finger pointing OUTSIDE your trail shoulder. The lead thumb sitting slightly on the trail side of the handle rather than straight down the top.

TRAIL HAND (right) MATCHES IT. Its palm faces the target and covers the lead thumb, and its own V runs roughly PARALLEL to the lead V. This is the half that gets skipped, and skipping it is worse than changing nothing: a strong lead hand under a trail hand still sitting on top of the handle is two hands trying to hold the face in two different places, and which one wins changes under pressure. Both hands rotate, or neither does.

PRESSURE stays light, and mostly in the last three fingers of the lead hand. A tight hold is how a grip change turns into an arm change.

WHAT IS NOT PART OF THIS: how the hands ATTACH to each other. Overlap, interlock and ten-finger are a separate choice and none of them makes a grip stronger or weaker. Keep whatever you use now, so rotation is the only thing that moved.

THE ONE CROSS-REFERENCE WORTH HOLDING: this is the OPPOSITE hold from your putting grip, on purpose. The putter runs up the LIFELINE to lock the wrists so they cannot hinge; a full-swing club sits in the FINGERS so they can. If your full-swing grip starts creeping into the palm, that is the putting hold leaking across. The putting one lives in the Putting lab's Grip & Posture plan, and nothing about it gets written here.

sections.t: PUT A NUMBER ON IT BEFORE YOU MOVE IT
sections.k: You cannot go from weak to strong without knowing which one you are on today — photograph it and write the knuckle count down.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS — the method this app already learned the hard way, applied to a new setting.

NOBODY HAS EVER LOOKED AT YOUR GRIP. There is no photograph, no film frame that reads knuckles, and no note anywhere in this app saying what your current hold is. So 'stronger' has no starting point, and that goes wrong two ways: you may already be neutral-to-strong and about to overshoot, or you move it and have no way of saying how far you went.

The app has been here before. 'Barely open' was the putter face cue for a month with no number on it, and it could not be checked, defended or reproduced — the plans still carry the guard about it. Same shape of problem, same fix: measure the thing before you move it.

SO: photograph the grip first, from directly above your hands, looking down the way your eyes do at address, on a club you actually play. COUNT THE KNUCKLES IN THE PICTURE rather than by feel — a grip is one of the places where feel and reality come apart fastest, and feel is the least reliable instrument in this app. Write the number down. There is a standing to-do for it on the Coach board.

THEN MOVE ONE KNUCKLE, not two. If the picture says two and you want three, go to two and a half and live there for a week. A grip that jumps straight to its target is a grip that gets abandoned in the third round, the first time a ball goes left.

sections.t: WHAT A GRIP CHANGES, AND WHAT IT CANNOT TOUCH
sections.k: A grip moves where the FACE points; nothing about it moves where the club TRAVELS — and your open fault is a path fault.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE, applied to what is already on your card.

THE MECHANISM. A strong lead hand does not close the face by itself. What it changes is what a NEUTRAL, unforced arrival looks like: with the hand rotated clockwise at address, the lead wrist returning to flat through impact delivers a face pointing further left than it used to. That is exactly why the release feels easier — you no longer have to rotate anything actively to square it, which is the benefit you named.

WHAT THAT MAKES IT: a FACE lever. And face is the powerful one for direction — standard teaching puts roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of a shot's START direction on where the face points at impact, with the curve coming from the difference between face and path. That is somebody else's measurement, off launch monitors, not one of yours; you have never been on one.

WHAT IT CANNOT DO. Nothing about how you hold the club changes where the club TRAVELS. Path comes from body, plane and sequence. Your open fault 'over the top' is a path fault — out to in — and a strong grip leaves it exactly where it is while cancelling its curve. What that produces is a ball starting left of target that does not fade back.

AND THIS HAS ALREADY HAPPENED TO YOU ONCE. In June the driver went from a stiff shaft to a regular one, the curve largely disappeared and the miss became two-way. The Workshop Log's Aug 31 section is explicit about what that was: a shaft that lets the face square, cancelling a path fault's curve without touching the path. That is a face-side cancellation, and it is already in place.

SO THE GUARD IS ABOUT STACKING, and it is the same one the Putting lab carries about eye dominance: treat the strong grip as ONE face-side lever on a path nobody has corrected, never as a second correction on top of the shaft. Two face-side fixes stacked on one uncorrected out-to-in path is how a slice becomes a pull-hook — a worse miss than the one you have, because it starts at trouble instead of finishing there. The gate below is what catches that if it happens.

sections.t: WHAT YOUR OWN CARDS SAY — and how thin it is
sections.k: On the only card in this app recording tee-shot directions the miss went LEFT more often than right, so nothing here measured a slice.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS — your own scorecards, and the honest size of them.

ONE CARD IN THIS APP RECORDS WHERE TEE SHOTS FINISHED: Sterling Farms, Aug 12 2026, 18 holes. Fourteen holes recorded a fairway. Six were hit. The eight misses went FIVE LEFT, TWO RIGHT and one short.

WHAT THAT IS WORTH, said plainly because a number this small can mislead on its own. It is one round. It records where the ball FINISHED, not whether it started there or curved there — so it cannot tell a pull from a hook, or a push from a slice. It predates the Sep 8 bag switch. And it says nothing about which club was in your hands on any of those holes.

WHAT IT STILL SAYS: nothing in this app's own record shows you have a right-miss problem right now. The slice is your own lifelong read, which is exactly how it is filed on the diagnosis card — 'your own read', the weakest evidence tier there is, and it says so out loud rather than dressing itself up as measured.

AND THE LIVE CARDS ARE NOT IN THIS TEXT. Everything you have logged in the live logger since Aug 20 sits on your phone and outranks all of the above. The OFF THE TEE table in Rounds is always current and this page never will be, so read the table rather than this paragraph when you want to know which way the ball is actually going.

WHAT FOLLOWS. Build the grip because a repeatable, checkable hold is worth owning and yours has never been looked at. That reason survives whichever way the ball is going this month. 'It fixes my slice' does not survive your own record.

sections.t: THE DRIVER IS SET — which makes it a control
sections.k: The weight is dialled and stays put, so a shape change after the grip change has exactly one candidate.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, corrected Sep 9 2026.

THE WEIGHT IS DIALLED. You set it at Wianno, it is where you want it, and it is not moving. So the slider job came off the Aug 31 driver to-do; what is left on it is READING the club, which is a different job and still worth doing — the sleeve setting, the shaft band and the playing length are three build facts nobody has ever written down.

WHY THAT HELPS HERE, rather than just being one less thing to do. A setting that is not moving is a CONTROL. If the ball starts drawing more once the grip changes, the grip did it — there is no second variable to blame and no argument to have with yourself about which one it was.

SO KEEP IT THAT WAY: do not touch the slider while the grip is bedding in, even if the shape moves on you. If it moves too far, the answer is in the grip — back it off half a knuckle — not in the sole of the driver. You already paid for that setting once, at a course where it worked.

sections.t: THE GATE — how you will know, and when to back it off
sections.k: Judge it on the divot and the face tape; ball flight is the least reliable witness there is for compression.
sections.b:
SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE in the tests, YOURS in the pass marks.

EVERY GRIP CHANGE FEELS WRONG FOR TWO WEEKS. That is adaptation, not information, so feel cannot be the judge. And for compression specifically the BALL FLIGHT is the least reliable witness on offer — a flipped iron and a compressed one both find greens. Three things tell the truth and all three are free.

THE DIVOT. It starts AT or AFTER the ball, never before. Look at every divot for a fortnight; that one habit is worth more than anything else on this page, and it is the single measurement nobody can argue with. The drill that puts a line on the ground for it is on the bench.

THE FACE. Foot spray or impact tape, one range session a fortnight. A strike low on the face or out on the toe does not compress whatever your hands did — and if that is what is happening, the grip was never the problem and this plan is the wrong page.

THE FLIGHT, read the right way round. A compressed iron flies LOWER and goes FURTHER, with more spin. If the flight gets HIGHER and shorter after the grip change, you have added loft — the flip is still in there and the grip has not reached it.

GIVE IT THREE WEEKS before any verdict, and then the DIRECTION GUARD, which is the other half of the gate and the reason the slice material in this plan is still here.

TOOK, AND WORKING — the ball starts on line or a touch right and holds, or draws gently, and the divots start after the ball. Keep it.

TOO STRONG FOR YOUR PATH — the ball starts LEFT and curves further LEFT. That is the pull-hook the sections above warn about, and the answer is to BACK THE GRIP OFF half a knuckle. Not to aim right, not to hold the face open, not to add anything: a compensation on top of a compensation is the opposite of what a simpler grip was for.

HAS NOT TAKEN — nothing moved, in the divots or the flight. Check the TRAIL hand first, because it is the half that gets skipped, and check the photograph rather than the feel.

ON THE COURSE the app is already counting the part it can see: log the tee club and the approach club, and the Off the tee and Into the green tables do the rest. They cannot see a strike, which is why the divot is the one you watch yourself.

The drills are on the Coach bench — 'Build the grip the same way every time' at home, 'Read the strike, not the feel' at the range for the compression test, and the ball-first divot-line drill for the divot itself. They live there rather than here because the bench is the one place drills are allowed to be.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where this plan came from, and the six weeks a putting verdict spent sitting on a swing page.
sections.b:
Sep 9 2026 — plan created from your ask for a stronger left hand, then REFRAMED the same day when you said what it was for: compression, not the slice. The first cut led with the textbook's headline and reasoned against the miss the app already had on file; that material is still here as the guard on how far to take the change, which is what it is good for. The full working is in the Swing Workshop Log's Sep 9 section, including the correction.

ALSO CORRECTED Sep 9: the driver's sliding weight is dialled — set at Wianno, no change wanted. The first cut of this plan worked out an ordering between the grip and that slider, which was moot. The to-do kept its reading jobs and lost the slider job.

THE GRIP EXPERIMENT (Jul 2026) was a PUTTING plan — conventional against left-hand-low against the claw, run on the DF3i — and conventional won it. It was retired into the putting plans when they were reorganised, and it has nothing to do with the full-swing hold. Worth saying because its verdict leaked: 'Grip settled: conventional' sat in the FOCUS line of Swing Thoughts — Club by Club from Jul 26 until Sep 9, on a full-swing page, six weeks after the putting section it was written for had moved out to the Putting lab. Fixed in the same push that created this plan.

SOURCES. The strong-grip description — knuckle count, V direction, fingers over palm, the pros and cons — came from you, and it is mainstream teaching rather than anything measured here; the links you sent are video and swing-tip pages and are not treated as evidence by this plan. The face-versus-path mechanism and the start-direction split are standard launch-monitor teaching, labelled STANDARD PRACTICE wherever they appear because they are somebody else's numbers. The miss counts are your Sterling Farms card, Aug 12 2026. The shaft history and the two-way miss are your own report, recorded Aug 31 and unmeasured.

STILL UNMEASURED, and this is the honest limit of the whole plan: your current grip (no photograph exists), your club path and face-to-path (no launch-monitor session has ever happened), and whether the June shaft change moved the path or only the curve. The grip you can settle this week with a phone. The other two need a sim, and that to-do has been open since Aug 20.

briefing.text: SWING FILM — FOUR FIXES, PRICED OFF YOUR OWN LAKESIDE CLIP (Sep 9 2026). The video behind the Aug 17 stills was measured frame by frame. The camera is BEHIND you, which is half of what the across-the-line top needs — but behind is not the same as square down the line, and nothing in the frame establishes the azimuth, so the rear-quarter reading on that session stands and the top is still not gradeable. Four fixes, all cheap, and together they are the difference between a good-looking clip and one that closes a fault open since July. (1) PUT AN ALIGNMENT STICK DOWN THE TARGET LINE, in frame. This is the big one: across the line and laid off are angles measured AGAINST the target line, and nothing in that clip says where the target line is. No zero, no angle. (2) PROP THE PHONE, do not hold it — the background drifted 30 px across 8 seconds, so the reference moves during the swing. Lean it on the bag. (3) HAND HEIGHT, not head height. Apparent shaft plane moves with camera height, which is exactly why hand height is the standard. (4) 240 fps, not 60. At 60 the driver head covers about two and a half feet between frames, so there is no impact frame at all — and tempo needs 120 as a floor before the ratio means anything. Also: keep the whole club in frame, it reached the left edge at the top. SWING — THE ONE SET OF FILM THAT PAYS THREE WAYS. Widened Sep 9 2026: the grip change is aimed at COMPRESSION, and compression is low point and shaft lean — both of which live in the same face-on frame this to-do already wanted. Swing film exists — Jul 19 in a sim bay, Jul 26 stills, and the Aug 17 Lakeside clip the stills came from — and not one of them has ever produced a number AT IMPACT. This set would be the first. SHOOT IT LIKE THIS: face-on, SQUARE to you, lens at KNEE height, 240fps slo-mo, an alignment stick on the ground in frame for scale, OUTDOORS OFF TURF, five reps with a 7-iron — then one down-the-line from ON the target line at hand height. WHAT IT CLOSES: low point (fitted across the impact window, and cross-checked against where the divot actually starts — that anchor is free and the film cannot argue with it), attack angle with honest error bars, a tempo baseline, and the address posture below. WHAT IT CANNOT: face angle and dynamic loft at impact — at 240fps the head moves six inches between frames, so impact falls between two of them. Those are launch-monitor numbers and they are on the sim to-do. SWING — POSTURE, and the film that can actually grade it. The Aug 17 driver stills show a rounded upper back and chin on the chest at address, a trail leg that straightens at the top, and a body taller through delivery than at address — so the 'lose it through contact' feel is posture, not stalling hips: the finish is complete. Two things. (1) MIRROR CHECK at address: hinge from the hips, chest tall, a fist between chin and chest, and hold a little trail-knee flex to the top. (2) NEXT RANGE SESSION, film SQUARE down the line — phone on the ground ON the target line behind the ball, at hand height — plus one face-on. The Aug 17 angle was rear-quarter, which is why the across-the-line top still has not been re-graded since Jul 26.
briefing.note: Film date corrected to Aug 17 — the Aug 20 Lakeside ROUND is a separate event and is not what this film came from.

briefing.focus: Everything inside about six feet. The GRIP is SETTLED as of Sep 10 — the CLAW, every short putt, your call — so it is what you play now rather than something you are trying. That leaves ONE dial still open, the POP STROKE (short back, short through, shoulders not wrists), and it makes the test simpler than it has ever been: claw on both blocks, and the stroke is the only thing that changes. The 20-ball five-footer decides that one. Past six feet is the Lag Putts plan, and the grip goes back to conventional there.
rules: CLAW inside ~6 FEET — settled Sep 10, your call. Not a trial, not a fallback
CONVENTIONAL past 6 feet — the grip now changes at the same line the stroke does
IF YOU ARE UNSURE WHICH SIDE OF SIX YOU ARE ON, IT IS A LAG — go conventional
ONE dial still open: the POP STROKE. Both blocks claw, stroke is the only change
SHORT BACK, SHORT THROUGH — but still ACCELERATING through the ball
SHOULDERS, NOT WRISTS — the classic pop is a wrist stroke, and that one is not available to you
17 INCHES PAST is the speed — firm enough to hold line, not a jam
SHAFT VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT — a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it
It cures the TRAIL HAND, not AIM — barely open still does the aiming
SHORT ≠ QUITTING. If the short ones come up short, that is deceleration, not the plan
ADOPTED BY DECISION, NOT BY MEASUREMENT — the 20-ball five-footer is still owed

sections.t: THE GRIP IS SETTLED — one dial left
sections.k: Grip is decided and stroke shape is not, so the four-combination test collapses to two blocks that differ by exactly one thing.
sections.b:
FROM YOU, Sep 10 2026, and authoritative: the claw from now on for short putts, maybe six feet and less. That is a decision about what you DO, so it is the instruction on this card from today. It is not waiting on a scoreboard and it is not on trial — this plan stops describing two candidates and starts describing one grip and one open question.

WHAT IT CHANGES ABOUT THE TESTING, which is the useful half. Grip and stroke shape were two independent dials, which gave four combinations and an order to work through them in. One of those dials is now FIXED. So the experiment collapses from four blocks to two, and BOTH OF THEM ARE CLAW:

1. CLAW + your normal stroke length — the new baseline. Everything gets measured against this from here.
2. CLAW + the pop stroke.

Same session, same green, same day, and the only thing that differs between the blocks is the stroke. That is what makes a result mean something. The error that ran through the whole putter saga was four head movements in twelve days with more than one thing changed on every one of them, and fixing the grip is the single cheapest way to stop repeating it.

THE OLD BASELINE IS GONE, and that is worth saying out loud rather than quietly rolling it forward. Every conventional-grip short-putt number in this project was made with a different grip, and the best of them — 8 out of 10 from four feet, Jul 20, still the only scored putting benchmark anywhere in the record — was also made with a different putter. Those are history, not a target. THE FIRST CLAW BLOCK YOU RUN IS THE BASELINE, and until you run it this plan has no scoreboard at all.

WHAT IS STILL NOT DECIDED. The pop stroke, and the sections below still describe an experiment. The two were always aimed at different failures: the pop attacks DECELERATION and the freeze, by giving a conscious mind less time and less room to intervene; the claw attacks the TRAIL HAND. Settling one does not answer the other.

AND THE ONE THAT IS SETTLED MAKES THE ONE THAT ISN'T SAFER TO RUN. A firm short hitting stroke is exactly the shape that invites the trail hand to take over, and the claw is the physical guard against that — the trail hand is off the handle before you start. When the pop was going to be tested on a conventional grip, the guard was discipline. Now it is geometry. That is a real upgrade to the experiment and not just a reordering of it.

sections.t: SIX FEET — where the line actually falls
sections.k: Six is the line this plan already drew and the app already counts to, so the boundary needs no new judgment — and where there is doubt it falls to conventional.
sections.b:
Your words were "maybe 6ft and less", and the hedge is fair: nobody paces a putt off before deciding how to hold the club. What makes six workable is that it is not a new number. This plan has been quarantined inside about six feet since Aug 13, the Lag Putts plan starts past it, and the app's own putting buckets break in exactly the same place — inside three feet, then four to six, then seven to twelve. So the claw's range is the two shortest buckets, and every putt you log already records which side of the line it was on. Nothing has to be added to the logger for this decision to become checkable.

THE DECISION RULE ON THE GREEN, because "about six feet" is a judgment and you make it standing over the ball with no tape measure. IF YOU ARE UNSURE, IT IS A LAG — go conventional. The asymmetry is real and it runs one way. The cost of a claw on a putt that turns out to be long is a distance-feel trade made on the exact shot where pace is your open fault. The cost of conventional on a putt that turns out to be short is that you held it the way you have held it all year. One of those two mistakes lands on the thing you are trying to measure; the other does not. Let the doubt fall toward conventional.

WHAT WOULD MOVE THE LINE. Only the scoreboard. If claw blocks come back better at eight and ten feet as well, then six is the wrong number and it moves — but it moves on MAKES, not on how the grip feels out there, because a claw that feels good at ten feet is precisely how a distance-feel trade gets made without anybody noticing it happened.

sections.t: WHAT THE POP STROKE ACTUALLY IS
sections.k: A short backstroke and a firm rap with little follow-through — and it was invented for slow greens, which is what you play.
sections.b:
The pop stroke is a short backstroke, a firm accelerating rap at the ball, and an abbreviated follow-through. Gary Player played it, rapping the ball with almost no finish. Billy Casper is the purest example — compact, hands close to the body, the face hooded going back, and then a pop; the standard description is that it looks like tapping a tack with a hammer, which is why it is also called the tap stroke.

The part worth knowing before you adopt it: this stroke came out of SLOW GREENS. It was developed by players who needed extra pop to get the ball to the hole on surfaces that did not run. That is a genuine argument in its favour for you — your pace is calibrated at an estimated 8-9 stimp, which is exactly that world. It is also the warning that comes with it. On a fast green a stroke built to add force is the wrong instinct, and you will find that out on a downhill four-footer before you find it out anywhere else.

Your own description of it — short back, SHORT through — is the same shape Casper played, minus the mechanism that made it work for him. It describes the SIZE of the stroke and nothing about the hands, which is exactly the half worth borrowing.

sections.t: THE ONE THING YOU CANNOT COPY — the wrists
sections.k: Casper's pop was a wrist stroke; on this putter it has to be a short shoulder stroke instead, or it fights everything else you do.
sections.b:
This is the whole adaptation, and it is not a small one. The classic pop stroke is a WRIST stroke. Casper cocked his wrists to keep the face square going back and then released them into the ball. The technique's own history says as much: it was right-wrist action that supplied the extra pop on slow greens.

That mechanism is not available to you, for two reasons that point the same way. Your whole method is QUIET HANDS with the shoulders running the stroke. And the head you play is built on the premise that the face squares ITSELF when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own instruction is that your job is only to let it stay square. A wrist-released pop is the single most hand-active stroke in putting. Bolting it onto a zero-torque putter is asking the club to undo what you are doing to it.

So take the GEOMETRY, not the MECHANISM. Short backstroke, short through-stroke — your call, and it is the authentic shape; Casper's finish stopped dead. Both halves run from the shoulders, with the wrists silent — exactly the stroke you already make, just shorter and more committed. What you are borrowing from Casper is the SIZE and the INTENT, and nothing else.

The tell that you have drifted into the real thing is the putter head PASSING YOUR HANDS. That is the wrist releasing, and it is the one thing to watch for — though it got harder to do on Sep 10, because the claw is back in play as the running grip and a trail hand that is off the handle cannot flip the one it is not holding. The guard used to be discipline. It is geometry now. Watch for it anyway: a claw makes the flick awkward rather than impossible, and awkward is not the same as gone.

sections.t: SHORT THROUGH IS NOT THE SAME AS QUITTING
sections.k: A short finish that accelerated and a short finish that decelerated look identical afterwards — the ball's roll-out is what tells them apart.
sections.b:
This is the one thing to get right about a short finish, because the good version and the bad version leave the same picture.

THE GOOD ONE: the head accelerates through the ball and then stops, because the stroke was small and the energy went into the ball. That is Casper's stroke, and it is what you have asked for.

THE BAD ONE: the head slows down BEFORE the ball and the finish is short because there was nothing left. That is deceleration — the classic short-putt killer, and the thing a short backstroke makes easy to fall into, since a small backstroke gives you less room to build any speed at all.

Afterwards they look the same. So do not judge it by the finish. JUDGE IT BY THE ROLL-OUT: a stroke that accelerated gets the ball consistently to 17 inches past. A stroke that quit leaves putts short and, worse, leaves them short by a varying amount. If your short putts start finishing at the front edge, the through-stroke is quitting, and the fix is committing to the pace rather than lengthening the backstroke.

The useful mental version: the backstroke sets the size, the through-stroke sets the INTENT. Short is a size. Quitting is a loss of intent, and it is a different thing entirely.

sections.t: SPEED — 17 inches past, and why firm is right on the short ones
sections.k: The ring around the hole is trodden flat, so a dying ball wobbles through it — 17 inches past is the researched target.
sections.b:
There is a real reason a firmer short putt works, and it is not toughness. The area roughly one to six feet all around a hole takes all the foot traffic on a green, so it is depressed and bumpy — Dave Pelz's 'lumpy donut'. A ball arriving with barely any pace wobbles through exactly the bit of green that is in the worst condition. A ball with a little more speed pushes through it.

Pelz's number is 17 INCHES PAST the hole. That is the target: enough pace to hold the line through the trodden ring and take some break out, not so much that you shrink the effective hole and leave yourself the one coming back.

The honest counter-argument, because it is real physics: a ball dying into the hole can fall in off the edges, so a softer putt has a bigger effective target and more room for a stroke error. Both things are true. The reason firm wins on a SHORT putt specifically is that inside six feet you are not solving a distance problem — you are trying to start it on line and get it there before the green can do anything to it. That balance flips as soon as the putt gets long, which is why this stroke is quarantined.

17 inches is a specific number, so treat it as one: on the practice green, put a tee 17 inches behind the hole and putt to leave it between the hole and the tee.

sections.t: THE LOFT TRAP — when the rap becomes a jab
sections.k: A firm short stroke is the easiest way to lean the shaft forward, and this face has 2° to give before the ball is being driven into the turf.
sections.b:
This is the specific way the pop stroke can hurt you on THIS putter, and it is worth more attention than the stroke shape.

Casper's pop hit the ball and then the turf, clubhead stopping abruptly. That is a descending, forward-leaning delivery. Your putter is built around 0° shaft lean, so a rap arriving with the shaft leaning forward delofts a face that has little to lose — and a delofted putt is driven into the turf: it skids, then rolls, and finishes short and off line.

Its loft is 2°, CONFIRMED — L.A.B. publishes 2° effective loft for this head in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the LINK.2.1 custom build page — confirmed Aug 14, so this is a spec now, not an inference. The arithmetic is no longer directional: you have 2° to spend and a forward-leaning delivery spends it fast. This section was written when the figure was an inference; the number came back the same, which is why nothing it told you to do has changed.

The rule does not relax because the stroke got shorter. SHAFT VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT — the same on this stroke as on every other one.

AND AS OF SEP 10 THERE ARE TWO SUSPECTS ON THIS CARD AGAIN. Between Aug 25 and Sep 10 there was one: the forward press had come out — the trigger is a re-grip, which moves pressure rather than the shaft — leaving the pop as the only move that could lean this face forward. The claw is the second one. It leans the shaft in a way you do not feel, where the pop leans it in a way you might, so they fail differently and they are not interchangeable suspects. Both live on this card and nowhere else, which is why the scuff is worth listening for here more than anywhere on the green. This is an honest step BACKWARDS in diagnostic cleanliness, and it is the price of the decision rather than an argument against it.

The check needs no camera: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click. A driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you start hearing the scuff on short putts, the pop has turned into a jab and the shaft is leaning. The camera version is the same face-on clip you already owe — shaft angle at address against shaft angle at impact, same number both times.

sections.t: THE CLAW — what you now play
sections.k: Adopted by your decision on Sep 10: it takes the trail hand out, which is what makes 'quiet hands' mechanical rather than voluntary on a head built for exactly that.
sections.b:
SETTLED, your words, Sep 10 2026: the claw from now on inside about six feet. It is the grip on this card. It is no longer one of two candidates and it was never a fallback — that distinction mattered while it was being tested, because a candidate gets a deliberate block on the scoreboard where a fallback only ever gets reached for in a bad moment, which is the worst possible time to judge a grip. Now it gets neither: it gets played.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES. The claw takes the trail hand OUT of the stroke — pressure moves into the lead hand, the right becomes a guide, and flipping the wrists gets physically awkward rather than merely discouraged. That is a mechanical version of 'quiet hands', which is why it suits this putter. On this head, QUIET HANDS AND CLAW ARE THE SAME INSTRUCTION.

WHY IT FITS THIS PUTTER AT ALL. A zero-torque head is built on the premise that the face squares itself once the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is only to let it stay square, and their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. The claw exists to take a hand out. The head and the grip are asking for the same thing.

WHAT IT ANSWERS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The claw attacks the TRAIL HAND. Putts pushed or flicked off line are its problem to solve. Putts dying short and tentative are NOT — that is deceleration, that is the stroke, and a grip will not fix it. That is the pop stroke's question and it is still open.

WHAT IT COSTS, so the trade stays on the record rather than getting lost now that the decision is made. A CLAW TRADES A LITTLE DISTANCE FEEL FOR LINE CONTROL. That is a good trade inside six feet, where there is barely any distance problem to solve, and the wrong trade on a lag while pace is your open fault — which is why it stops at six feet rather than becoming your grip. Keeping it off the lags is also what keeps the 30-ft ladder numbers clean.

THERE IS NO FEEL HAND ON THE CLAW, and there should not be. The lag cue about the trail hand sensing the weight of the head is a CONVENTIONAL-GRIP cue that belongs to the Lag Putts plan, and it does not come in here. Inside six feet there is no distance to feel; the trail hand is a guide and nothing else. That used to be a note about what would happen if the claw came back. It is live now.

THE ONE CHECK THAT COMES WITH IT, and it is the reason the shaft rule on this card got sharper rather than looser today. A CLAW CAN PUSH THE HANDLE FORWARD WITHOUT YOU FEELING IT — the trail hand sits differently and the handle creeps. On a face with 2° of loft that drives the ball into the turf. So get BOTH grips into the same face-on set, white tape on the shaft, and compare shaft angle at address against shaft angle at impact. Vertical on both is the pass. Do not trust how it feels: the whole point of a claw is that your hands are somewhere unfamiliar, which is exactly when a feel is worth least.

WHAT THE SCOREBOARD IS FOR NOW. It has changed jobs. The 20-ball five-footer is no longer deciding whether to adopt the claw — you decided that — it is establishing what the claw is worth so that everything after it has something to be measured against. Run it claw. If it comes back worse than you expect, that is information and it is yours to act on or ignore; what it is not is a vote.

sections.t: WHY THIS STAYS INSIDE SIX FEET
sections.k: The pop holds the backstroke short and varies force, which is the exact failure the lag plan exists to prevent.
sections.b:
Your distance system says DISTANCE COMES FROM STROKE LENGTH AT A FIXED TEMPO. The Lag Putts plan names the opposite as the failure mode by name: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else.

A pop stroke is that failure mode, deliberately. It holds the length short and supplies the rest with force.

On a short putt that is not a flaw, because there is no meaningful distance problem to solve inside six feet — the ball has one job, which is to reach the hole on line. On anything longer it is exactly the thing that produced a round of short lags and hot short putts, and it is why pace has never been calibrated in this project.

So the split is hard: inside about six feet is this plan, outside it is the Lag Putts plan. Keeping them apart is what keeps the ladder numbers clean — the ladder is measuring the long stroke, and a pop rep on it is a corrupted data point.

AND AS OF SEP 10 TWO THINGS CHANGE AT THAT LINE, NOT ONE. Until today the grip was conventional on both sides and only the stroke shape changed at six feet. Now the grip changes there too. One consequence is worth stating because a plan elsewhere used to claim the opposite: THE SHORT-PUTT NUMBERS AND THE LADDER NUMBERS ARE NO LONGER DIRECTLY COMPARABLE. They are two grips as well as two stroke lengths, so a difference between them cannot be attributed to either. That claim has been removed from the Lag Putts plan rather than left standing. Each side of the line now has to be measured against itself — which is fine, because that is how both of them were always going to be used.

sections.t: WHAT IT FIXES, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T
sections.k: Between them they cure deceleration, the freeze and the trail hand — neither of them cures your aim.
sections.b:
WHAT IT GENUINELY HELPS. Deceleration, which is the classic short-putt killer, and the freeze — a short committed stroke gives the conscious mind less time and less room to intervene. That connects to the trigger work: your failure lives on short putts under pressure, not on the practice green, and a stroke with less dwell and less distance to travel is a real answer to that.

WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH, and this matters because it would be easy to expect otherwise. Your left miss is an AIM error, not a delivery error — reclassified Aug 10, and the Aug 10 pm mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right with no bias at all. Face angle decides about 80% of where a putt starts. A pop stroke changes how the face is DELIVERED; it does not change where you have AIMED it. Barely open is still what does the aiming, and it is untouched by any of this.

So do not expect the left ones to stop — and that goes for the claw exactly as much as for the pop. A grip change moves where the hands are; it does not move where you have AIMED. The claw is worth playing because it takes the trail hand out of a stroke this putter does not want a hand in, and the pop is worth testing because a short committed stroke under pressure is worth having. Neither is worth anything as an answer to the left miss, which is barely open's job and is untouched by any of this.

sections.t: THE SCOREBOARD — the 20-ball five-footer
sections.k: Two blocks in the same session, both on the claw, differing only in the stroke — and the first block you run is the baseline, because the old one belonged to another grip.
sections.b:
This does not get decided on feel. The whole project's record on deciding putting things by feel is four putter movements in twelve days.

THE TEST. 20 balls from five feet, in two blocks in the SAME session: one block with the pop stroke, one with your normal stroke length. SAME GRIP ON BOTH, AND AS OF SEP 10 THAT GRIP IS THE CLAW. Same green, same day — green speed changes everything and a comparison across two sessions compares two greens.

AND RUN THE NORMAL-STROKE BLOCK FIRST, because it is now doing two jobs: it is one arm of the pop-stroke test AND it is the first claw number this project has ever had. Every short-putt figure on file was made conventional, so there is nothing behind you to compare against and this block is what the next one gets measured on.

WHAT TO LOG. Makes out of 20, and the direction of every miss. The left-miss pass mark the grip experiment set — 2 or fewer LEFT misses per 20 — still reads across, because it is a test of aim and aim did not change today. The MAKE count does not read across: it was set on a conventional grip and a different putter, so treat the first claw block's number as a starting point rather than a mark to beat. Note the green speed too.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CONVICT IT. More makes is the headline, but watch three other things. If the misses get LONGER — running well past — the pop is a jab and the loft trap has you. If putts come up SHORT, the through-stroke is quitting rather than merely being short, which is the failure mode a short finish invites. And if you start hearing the scuff, stop and check the shaft before you read the scores at all.

Run it at two green speeds before you commit. A stroke built for slow greens will flatter itself on a slow one.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where the stroke came from, what was adapted, and what has not been measured.
sections.b:
SEP 10 2026, FROM YOU AND AUTHORITATIVE: "Claw grip from now on for short putts. Maybe 6ft and less." The claw stops being one of two candidates and becomes the grip inside six feet. Four things followed from it in this plan, and one of them is a step backwards that is worth naming rather than burying. The four-block test order (baseline / pop only / claw only / both) collapsed to TWO blocks, both claw, differing only in the stroke — a genuinely better experiment. The pop stroke's wrist risk is now guarded by geometry rather than by discipline. The old conventional-grip baseline retired, including Jul 20's 8/10 from four feet, so this plan currently has NO scoreboard until the first claw block is run. And the LOFT TRAP went from one suspect back to two, because a claw can push the handle forward without you feeling it. Retired with the decision: the backstop trip-wire that would have brought the claw back off the shelf, and the reserve-grip framing across GRIP & POSTURE, the ROUTINE plan and LAG PUTTS. Adopted by DECISION, not by measurement — no claw rep has ever been filmed or scored on this putter.

Aug 25: the forward press came out by your decision (a re-grip trigger instead), so this plan's shaft rule goes back to ADDRESS AND IMPACT alongside the ROUTINE and GRIP & POSTURE plans, and the press-plus-pop pairing that the LOFT TRAP called the highest-risk on the card is down to the pop alone. The risk did not fall — the number of things that could be causing it did.

Aug 14, later: the 2° loft this plan's LOFT TRAP section is built on was confirmed from L.A.B.'s specifications, having been an inference since Jul 30. The estimate was right, so no instruction moved — the section now states it as a spec.

Aug 14: the forward press came back as the trigger, so this plan's shaft rule was re-scoped from 'address and impact' to IMPACT, matching the ROUTINE and GRIP & POSTURE plans. The pop-plus-press combination is now called out in the LOFT TRAP section as the highest-risk pairing on the card.

FROM YOU, Aug 13 2026, and authoritative: a pop stroke on the short ones — short back, SHORT through, and no wrists. Also from you, same day: the claw is out of play as the running grip. CORRECTED shortly after to 'another short-putt SOLUTION you are trying, not a safety net' — and SUPERSEDED on Sep 10, when it became the grip. Both of those framings are history now; the top of this file carries what stands. The plan was retitled off the pop stroke because of it: two candidates are on trial, and naming the plan after one of them made the other look like a contingency.

RESEARCHED. The pop stroke's history and mechanics: Gary Player rapped it with no follow-through; Billy Casper is the canonical version — compact, hands close to the body, face hooded going back, ball-then-turf contact and an abbreviated finish, described as tapping a tack with a hammer. Its origin is slow greens, where right-wrist action supplied the extra pop. The speed target comes from Dave Pelz's research: the 'lumpy donut' of trodden ground one to six feet around the hole, and 17 inches past as the optimal pace. The counter-argument — that a dying ball has a bigger effective hole — is real physics and is stated rather than buried.

ADAPTED, and this is the significant edit. The classic pop is a WRIST stroke, which contradicts both quiet hands and the zero-torque premise of the LINK. What survives here is the geometry — short backstroke, positive through-stroke — run from the shoulders. That is a reasoned adaptation, not something anyone measured.

REVISED SAME DAY. An earlier version of this plan had the through-stroke 'at least as long as the backstroke' and the claw running as the guardrail. Both were corrected by you: the finish is short, and the grip is conventional. The anti-deceleration guard therefore moved from LENGTH to ACCELERATION, which is the honest version anyway. The wrist-flick guard went to discipline with the claw out, and came back to geometry with it on Sep 10.

NOT MEASURED. All of it, and the claw joined the list on Sep 10 rather than leaving it. No pop-stroke rep and no claw rep has ever been filmed or scored on this putter, the 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK on either grip, and the face-on clip that would catch the shaft leaning forward is still owed — and is owed twice over now, because it is the only thing that can catch a claw creeping the handle forward. Until the scoreboard exists this plan describes an experiment, not a finding.

ADDED with that reframe, and RETIRED on Sep 10: the two-dials section at the top and its four-combination test order (baseline, pop only, claw only, both). Grip and stroke shape are still independent variables and changing two at once is still the error that ran through the entire putter saga — but with the grip settled there is only one variable left to move, so the same reasoning now produces two blocks instead of four.

briefing.focus: Everything that is true before the putter moves, in one place: how you stand, what is in your hands, where the ball is, and where the low point ends up. The GRIP now depends on the length of the putt — claw inside about six feet as of Sep 10, conventional past it — and everything else on this card is true on both. One mechanism runs through the rest of it — lead-side pressure pins the low point, the low point decides whether the ball rolls or hops, and ball position plus a vertical shaft decide where that low point meets the ball. Keep any feel that passes the four checks. The routine that sits on top of this is the Putting Routine plan.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
CLAW inside ~6 ft, CONVENTIONAL past it (Sep 10) — the grip changes at the six-foot line
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel — mark it
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO FORWARD PRESS (Aug 25) — the trigger is a RE-GRIP, so the shaft is VERTICAL at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
Pressure ~55/45 LEAD — its one job is pinning the low point
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS — it never pushes, and nothing releases

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off, and it is what switches the putter's technology on.
sections.b:
Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, ~2° effective loft — an estimate, see the Notes — 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: THE GRIP — what is actually in your hands
sections.k: Claw inside about six feet, conventional past it, light pressure on both — and the light pressure is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference.
sections.b:
TWO GRIPS, SPLIT AT SIX FEET. As of Sep 10 the CLAW is the grip inside about six feet and CONVENTIONAL is the grip past it — your decision, and the reserve framing that stood here from Aug 13 is retired. The claw's own detail lives in the SHORT PUTTS plan, because that is the only place it is played. What this card says about the grip is what is true on BOTH of them.

IF YOU ARE UNSURE WHICH SIDE OF SIX FEET YOU ARE ON, IT IS A LAG — conventional. The reasoning is in the Short Putts plan; the short version is that the claw's cost is a distance-feel trade, and pace is the open fault, so the doubt has to fall on the side that does not touch it.

LIGHT PRESSURE, and this is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference. A Lie Angle Balanced head is built so the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is only to let it stay square, and their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one.

THE ZERO-LEAN GRIP GEOMETRY. This putter carries a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED — zero built-in lean. The shaft stands vertical and your hands sit about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, and that is correct rather than something to fix. The DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue belonged to its Press Pistol 2°, which leaned the shaft for you; that grip went back with that putter and the cue died with it. Never carry it across.

THE TRAIL HAND — YOURS, CHECKED. You proposed this one: on LAGS, conventional grip, with the RIGHT hand sensing the weight of the head and the left just riding along. Keep it — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. It is not standard putting instruction, but it survived a check against L.A.B.'s own quiet-hands design, and the instruction you paired it with — 'let the head release' — was cut precisely because that half contradicts a zero-torque head. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on stroke length, and it has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward — which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. This is a LAG cue and a CONVENTIONAL-grip cue, and as of Sep 10 those are the same thing: inside six feet you are on the claw, the trail hand is off the handle, and there is no distance to feel anyway. Do not carry it in there.

AND THE CLAW HAS THE SAME FAILURE BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE. A conventional trail hand shoves the handle forward by pushing; a claw does it because the hand simply sits somewhere else on the grip and takes the handle with it. Neither one announces itself. That is why the face-on clip this plan keeps asking for now has to be shot on BOTH grips in the same set — one number, address against impact, on each.

sections.t: THE SETUP — the four checks
sections.k: Ball inside the lead heel · low point just behind it · shaft back to vertical · 55/45. Pass all four and keep your feel.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries little loft and is delivered at 0° lean, so there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

(1) BALL one to two ball-widths INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. Use the heel, not a body reference — a deep-bend posture moves your chest line; the heel doesn't move. Mark it on the mat.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact. This is what ball position is for.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started.

(4) PRESSURE about 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much you start steering.

If a feel you're comfortable in delivers all four, keep the feel. The checks are the rule; the feel is yours.

sections.t: WEIGHT AND THE LOW POINT — the mechanism under all of it
sections.k: Lead pressure pins where the stroke bottoms out, and hanging back adds loft you never asked for.
sections.b:
Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. Everything below follows from that, on any head.

Weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so the head arrives climbing hard with the shaft leaning away from the target. That adds loft you never asked for: the ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then rolls. Every bit of hop is energy that was supposed to become roll, so the putt arrives soft — and skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your pace stops being repeatable between surfaces.

The window on this head is narrow in both directions, because a putter's loft budget is small to start with. Lean away from the target and you add loft; lean toward it and you go below zero and drive the ball down. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a skidding ball that finishes short of what the stroke intended.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address and at impact
sections.k: Nothing moves you off vertical any more, so address is a real check again — and both ends have to read the same number.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND VERTICAL AT IMPACT. Impact is the end that matters, and address is a fair proxy for it again as of Aug 25: the forward press is out and the trigger is a RE-GRIP (it lives in the ROUTINE plan), which changes what is in your hands rather than where the shaft is. Nothing takes you off vertical on purpose any more, so nothing has to be given back — and the two ends reading the same number is the whole test. Forward at IMPACT delofts a face with little to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical at impact are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. SHOOT IT ON BOTH GRIPS since Sep 10 — same set, same session, claw and conventional — because a two-grip method needs two answers and the claw is the one nobody has ever looked at. Check without one: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

Two different variables, two different controls. Ball position is set by your FEET (check 1). Shaft lean at impact is set by your HANDS (check 3), and the target is zero.

A vertical shaft photographs as the hands sitting about 1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball (0.84") from face to centre, plus roughly half an inch from shaft axis to face on this riser-hosel blade. That's not a position to set; it's what 'hands over the head of the putter' produces on its own. If you try to put the hands somewhere, you're adding lean. Nothing in the routine asks you to any more, which is the point of a trigger that lives in your grip pressure instead.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: The blade tells you
sections.k: This head reports a bad strike instead of muffling it — use that, then measure.
sections.b:
A narrow blade carries less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds real distance and you can FEEL it. That makes your hands a better instrument on this putter than on a big mallet — a mediocre low point won't hide.

Use it, but don't stop there. The sound check costs nothing: one clean click is a rolling ball; a faint scuff a beat later is a driven one. The measurement is the tape test — twelve minutes, its own plan — and it's the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter's pace.

sections.t: Settle any change with data
sections.k: A/B it on the ladder and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: current feel. Block B: the change, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread; tighter spread wins, and that's the answer, not anyone's opinion.

FACE-ON CLIP — the one measurement this plan keeps asking for, and since Sep 10 it is TWO clips, one per grip: shaft angle at address versus impact (matching at address and impact is the pass, and as of Aug 25 that is the plain question again — nothing in the routine moves the shaft, and the grip has no built-in lean either, so whatever the tape shows IS your hands), where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps, camera at ball height square to the line.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the checks above.
sections.b:
SEP 10 2026 — the claw came back as the running grip inside about six feet, your call, so this plan's 'CONVENTIONAL, BOTH LENGTHS' rule is retired and the grip is now split at six feet. Everything else on this card is unchanged and is true on both grips: the bend, the ball position, the vertical shaft, the trail foot, the pressure, the low point. What DID change is what the owed face-on clip has to cover — two grips, two answers — because a claw can creep the handle forward without the hands reporting it, which is the same failure the trail-hand cue was already guarded against by a different route. The trail-hand feel cue is now explicitly a LAG cue only.

Aug 25: the forward press is out by your decision — a late release and re-grip instead — so this plan's shaft rule reverts to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, which is where it stood before Aug 14. The reasoning that re-scoped it to impact alone is not wrong and is not retired; it simply has nothing to act on while nothing moves the hands off vertical. New guard, and it belongs to this plan because this is where grip pressure lives: re-grip to the SAME LIGHT PRESSURE you released, because a firmer regrab is a trail hand back in the stroke.

Aug 14: the forward press returned by your decision, so this plan's 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule is retired and the shaft rule re-scoped to IMPACT. What did NOT change: the mechanism. A shaft still leaning at impact still delofts and still finishes short — the press is only safe because it recovers, and that recovery is UNFILMED. The face-on address-versus-impact clip is now the owed measurement rather than a nice-to-have.

The 'hands level or a touch ahead at impact' rule that used to be check 3 belonged to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° — a grip with lean built in — and left with that putter on Aug 10; on a 0°-lean build, hands ahead delofts and drives it. The press was removed the same day, which also retired the old 'keep it tiny' arithmetic. The ball-forward, weight-on-the-ball question was settled on the mat back in July; what this plan adds is the number (1–2 widths inside the lead heel) and the ground reference. This plan's forgiveness section flipped twice with the bag — the mallet that muffled a wandering low point is gone, which raises the stakes and sharpens the feedback. And the reason the plan exists at all: pace decided the fate of two putters on feel alone, with zero calibrated lag sessions behind any verdict.

Aug 13: this plan was assembled from the old 'Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point' plus the posture, shaft, trail-foot and grip sections that used to live in the Routine plan — they were all one subject, and the Routine plan is now only the routine. The tape test moved to the LAG PUTTS plan. Also Aug 13: the claw came OUT of play by your call, so grip was conventional on every length. That held until Sep 10, above.

Aug 13 — a correction to this plan's own arithmetic. The 2° of effective loft quoted throughout is an ESTIMATE. No retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a loft for the LINK.2.1, so it was inferred rather than looked up, and every de-lofting calculation downstream of it is softer than it read. The mechanism is unaffected — a forward-leaning shaft delofts a face that has little to spare, and a delofted putt skids — but the margin is not a measured quantity. Language across the plans was softened accordingly.

AUG 30 2026 — labelled the TRAIL HAND cue as Jack's own, checked against the manufacturer's design, under the new yours-versus-textbook rule. It read as handed-down instruction; it is his, and the half of it that was cut is why that distinction matters.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: read it from behind, rehearse beside the ball with the pace look last, aim the FACE barely open and build the stance to it, release and RE-GRIP, and go — same beat count every putt. No forward press: this trigger changes what is IN your hands rather than where the shaft is, so the shaft is vertical at address AND at impact. How you stand and what is in your hands is the GRIP & POSTURE plan; the short ones and the lags each have their own, and since Sep 10 they are two different GRIPS as well as two different strokes — claw inside about six feet, conventional past it.
rules: READ IT FIRST — pace before break. The how lives in the Reading plan
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Rehearse BESIDE the ball — ball-look first, HOLE-look last, always
TRIGGER = a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP, LAST thing before the takeaway — same slot, same LIGHT pressure, and re-set into the grip you are PLAYING
Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is a pace variable
CLAW and POP on the short ones, CONVENTIONAL and full length on the lags — each has its own plan
Setup and grip live in GRIP & POSTURE — get low, ball inside the lead heel, shaft vertical at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → RE-GRIP → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE READ — its own plan now
sections.k: What the putt is going to do, before you aim anything at it, moved to the Reading the Green plan.
sections.b:
Step one of this routine is still read it from behind — but the HOW moved out on Aug 14, the same way grip and the short stroke did.

The short version, so you are not left with nothing: behind the ball for the line, the low side for the amount, feet first on a green that looks flat, and pick the PACE before you read the break, because a putt has a different line at every speed. Past six feet the pace target is the Lag Putts circle; inside six it is seventeen inches past.

Everything else — grain, the pro side, the fall line, and the three minutes on the practice green that buy you the day's speed — is in Reading the Green.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square (your read, still unconfirmed)
sections.k: YOUR find, not the textbook's: set what reads to you as barely open — on this putter that should play as square. One check on a real green still owed; put a number on it and re-check monthly.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, AND NOT A TEXTBOOK INSTRUCTION — no putting method tells anyone to aim open. You arrived at this yourself, it is the load-bearing correction for your oldest miss, and it has not been measured on a real green. Treat it as your working setting rather than a fact.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS: aim the face square to the start line. That is universal, and it is not in dispute.

WHAT YOU FOUND: that setting the face to what reads to your eye as barely OPEN is what actually gets the ball started on line.
