Those are only in conflict if your eye and the face agree, and the whole point is that yours may not — the likely explanation is an aim error that predates every putter you have owned, so 'barely open' is the correction that cancels it and 'square' is what it produces.

SO: on this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact, and whatever you set is what the ball gets. Set it the same way every putt and trust it until something measures it. What is NOT established is the amount: 'barely' has no number on it yet, which is the next paragraph.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. That guard got sharper on Aug 13, because a laser is a Lane B instrument by nature: watch a green line on the carpet long enough and your eye recalibrates whether you asked it to or not. Use it to MEASURE and look at the number afterwards. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: the laser does this properly now — at six feet, 1.26 inches of offset is one degree, so ten balls filmed against a marked scale turns barely open into an average you can re-check monthly. An unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good. The indoor half of it can now be done any evening — the PUTTLAZR (Aug 13) reads the aim directly once it is calibrated to the FACE rather than the shaft, and the whole protocol is in Coach → At-Home Putting. Aim by feel, never at the beam.

Run the TWO-DROP TEST in the same session, since you are already in posture: drop a ball from your nose, then drop one from directly under your right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. You are same-side dominant — right hand, right eye — and that predicts a LEFT aim bias, which is your miss exactly. The gap says whether that is live for you at all, measured bent over rather than standing up, which is the only version that counts. It is a reading, NOT a second correction: barely-open already cancels whatever aims you left, and stacking a fix on top misses right. Full write-up is in the Workshop Log.

sections.t: GRIP & POSTURE — its own plan now
sections.k: How you stand, what is in your hands, ball position, the shaft and the low point all moved to one plan.
sections.b:
Everything that is true BEFORE the putter moves now lives in GRIP & POSTURE — THE SETUP: get low and why the bend matters, the conventional grip and light pressure, ball one to two widths inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, the vertical shaft at both ends, the trail foot back, lead-side pressure and the low point, and the trail hand's job on lags.

What stayed here is the ROUTINE: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger and the beat count. Those are the things you do in an order, every putt, and they are what this plan is for.

sections.t: SHORT PUTTS — they have their own plan now
sections.k: Everything inside about six feet — the claw, the pop stroke, the speed target and the scoreboard — lives in the Short Putts plan.
sections.b:
This plan is the stroke and the routine you run on every putt. The short ones have enough of their own content — a different grip, a different stroke shape and a different speed target — that they now have their own plan: SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE.

What moved there: the pop stroke (short back, short through), the CLAW — which as of Sep 10 is the grip you play inside about six feet rather than a reserve — the 17-inch speed target, the loft trap that comes with rapping a ball on this face, and the 20-ball five-footer.

THE ONE THING THAT REACHES BACK INTO THIS PLAN is the trigger. A re-grip is the last thing you do before the stroke, so on a short putt you are now re-gripping into a CLAW. See THE TRIGGER below — it is a live check rather than a note for later.

What stayed here, because it is true on every putt regardless of length: get low, ball position, the vertical shaft, barely open, trail foot back, the trigger, and the rehearsals.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the release and re-grip
sections.k: Your trigger is a late release and re-grip, deliberate and in the slot as of Aug 25; it is safe on this putter because it moves PRESSURE rather than position, which is also the thing it can get wrong.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 25: NO forward press. What you actually run is a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP — the hands come off the handle late and re-set on it — and then you go. Which trigger you run is yours to decide.

WHY THIS IS THE SAFE KIND OF TRIGGER ON THIS PUTTER. A re-grip changes what is in your hands, not where the shaft is. Nothing leans, so nothing has to be given back, and the 2° of effective loft this head is built to deliver at zero lean stays untouched (CONFIRMED Aug 14 from L.A.B.'s own specifications). That is what lets the shaft rule go back to what it was: VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, in this plan and in GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS. Address is a real check again, because nothing moves you off it.

THE GUARD THIS TRIGGER BRINGS WITH IT IS A DIFFERENT ONE. A press risked a POSITION; a re-grip risks a PRESSURE. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one, and re-gripping is by definition the moment you set it. So: RE-GRIP TO THE SAME LIGHT PRESSURE YOU RELEASED. If the regrab lands firmer than the grip you let go of, you have just put the trail hand back into a stroke this whole plan is built to keep it out of — and firmer hands is a quicker putt, which lands on the open fault. Nothing measures this but you, and a squeeze is one of the few things a feel reports honestly.

IT IS A DECISION NOW — your call, Aug 25, and FOR NOW is your framing and the honest one. You started from 'I kinda just do' it, which describes a habit, and a habit is the thing that goes missing exactly when you are hot or rushed, which is the moment a trigger exists for. So it is deliberate from here: the release and re-grip IS the trigger, it happens in the SAME SLOT every putt, and it is the LAST thing before the stroke starts. Provisional, held until something either measures it or you change your mind — nothing has filmed it, and none of the three triggers you have run since Aug 10 has ever been measured.

FOUR RULES for whichever trigger you run. ONE trigger, never two. SAME SLOT every putt — it is the last thing before the stroke. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — count the seconds you stand still over the ball; if a trigger hasn't shortened it, it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; walk back behind the ball and restart. Eight seconds, always cheaper than the putt.

AND NOW THAT IT IS A DECISION, IT CAN BE GRADED — cheaply, and this is the only trigger you have run that has ever had a number attached. A trigger has exactly one job: it gets you out of standing still. So COUNT THE DWELL. Ten putts, stopwatch or just a beat count, from your last look at the hole to the takeaway; write the average down. Do it once in the next session while the trigger is new, and again in a fortnight. If the number has not come down, the re-grip is decoration and you are running no trigger whatever it feels like. No camera, no kit, and it is the cheapest scoreboard on this plan.

AND THE LADDER IS STILL A DETECTOR, watching for something new. It used to watch for a press that leaked lean and finished putts SHORT; it now watches for a re-grip that arrives firm and sends them LONG. Either way the rule holds: if the 30-ft ladder starts showing a pattern it was not showing before, suspect the trigger before you suspect your pace.

THE CLAW CAME BACK OFF THE SHELF ON SEP 10, so this is a live check now and not a note for later. The trail hand sits differently in a claw, which means 're-set it the same way' is a DIFFERENT PHYSICAL ACT inside six feet than outside it, and the pressure it lands on is not the one your hands have spent the year learning. Three things follow.

RE-GRIP INTO THE GRIP YOU ARE PLAYING. The release-and-re-grip does not become a grip CHANGE — you take the claw before the routine starts, not during it. Deciding how to hold the putter is a decision, and a decision belongs behind the ball with the read, not in the last beat before the takeaway where the trigger lives.

THE SAME-LIGHT-PRESSURE RULE STILL HOLDS, and it is harder to obey in a claw because there is less hand on the club to report with. If anything, err lighter: the claw already takes the trail hand out mechanically, so a firm regrab is putting back the exact thing the grip was adopted to remove.

AND THE DWELL COUNT BELOW IS NOW TWO NUMBERS, not one. Count it on a short putt and on a lag. A trigger that shortens the dwell on one grip and not the other is telling you something, and there is no reason to assume it behaves the same in both.

The full shelf of alternatives — kinetic and sensory, and what each one costs — is in the Putting Workshop Log under Aug 13; Aug 14 carries the press reversal and the Aug 25 line on it carries this one.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training. REASONED, NOT SOURCED: that last step follows from where the arms hang in each posture. It is not a published finding and nobody has measured it on you — the ORDER below is the part that is standard teaching.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE STANDING WORK — where it lives
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet twice a week, and the whole protocol is in the Lag Putts plan.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only: 10 balls from 30 feet, logging SHORTS, SPREAD and GREEN SPEED, plus the 20/30/40 backstroke map. That is the standing work, and it belongs to pace rather than to the routine.

The full protocol, the targets and the tape test all live in the LAG PUTTS plan. The short-putt scoreboard — the 20-ball five-footer — lives in SHORT PUTTS.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.
sections.b:
SEP 10 2026 — the claw is the grip inside about six feet, your call. Nothing about the ROUTINE itself changed: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger slot and the beat count are the same on every putt regardless of what is in your hands. What changed is one live check — the re-grip trigger now lands in two different grips depending on the length of the putt, and the note that used to say 'if the claw ever comes back' is a check rather than a hypothetical. Also: the dwell count that grades the trigger is now two numbers, short and long.

Aug 25, later: the release and re-grip is a DECISION now rather than a habit you noticed — your call, and held provisionally. What that buys is a check: a trigger's one job is shortening the dwell, so the dwell count became the owed measurement and went on the trigger to-do. It is the first time a trigger in this project has had a number attached to it at all.

Aug 25: the FORWARD PRESS is out, your call — you run a late release and re-grip instead, and no press at all. Because a re-grip moves PRESSURE rather than position, the vertical-shaft rule reverted from 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' back to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT across this plan, GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS — changed in one pass so there is one live source. The owed press clip closed with it: there is no press left to film, and the face-on clip it was folded into got easier to grade rather than harder. The guard changed shape too — it is pressure now, not position. Adopted on FEEL and UNFILMED, exactly like the two triggers before it, which is the third time in fifteen days; the Workshop Log's Aug 14 section keeps its finding and carries a SINCE UPDATED line rather than being rewritten.

Aug 14, later: the loft was confirmed at 2° from L.A.B.'s specifications, so the trigger section no longer calls it an estimate. Nothing about the press changed — a confirmed-small loft budget makes the case for a press that RECOVERS slightly stronger, not weaker.

Aug 14: the FORWARD PRESS came back, your call — you tried the shelf and it felt best of them all. It replaces the trail-thumb press, which was only ever yours by decision too and was never filmed. The Aug 10 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule and this plan's own 'forward press stays out permanently' line are both gone; the vertical-shaft rule was re-scoped from 'address AND impact' to 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' across the Routine, GRIP & POSTURE and SHORT PUTTS plans, so there is only one live source. Adopted on FEEL and UNMEASURED — this project's own worked example is 'pace felt dialled' (Aug 1), which un-benched a putter that went back nine days later.

Aug 10: the press came out (your call — the 2° loft budget has nothing to spare, and a varying press is a varying pace). The DF3i was returned for distance control; its Press Pistol 2° went with it, and every 'hands even / hands ahead' cue died with that grip. The claw reopened for shorts — the old 'claw shelved' verdict came from a different putter, a different grip and a live left miss, so it doesn't bind. 'Hands over the ball' was corrected to 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' — the corrected version matches the Jul 30 stills exactly (vertical shaft = hands ~1.35" behind the ball centre), the first time a feel and a measurement have landed on each other in this project.

Aug 10 pm film: three putts on a lined mat went 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — the one-way LEFT pull from Jul 30 (1.5°, 1.7°) did not reproduce. Start line downgraded; the residual dispersion points at strike, not aim; the old 0.5° gate is retired as too strict for the player and the method.

Jul 30 film, still standing: SBST path confirmed across four putters; tempo 2.0:1; early lift closed; stance line closed (toes never open); vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°. Pace remains the open fault — it decided the fate of two putters without ever being measured, which is why the ladder is the standing work.

Aug 13 — two workshops, both written up in full in the PUTTING WORKSHOP LOG rather than here. THE TRAIL HAND: the L.A.B. framing checked out, 'let the head release' did not and was cut, and the lead-hand half was scoped to the lags because the claw inverts it. THE TRIGGER: the trail thumb press is yours by decision, and the old 'NO PRESS' rule was renamed NO FORWARD PRESS to kill the collision. Neither has been filmed — that the thumb press leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

Aug 13, later: the setup and grip sections moved out to GRIP & POSTURE and the claw section moved to SHORT PUTTS, leaving this plan as the routine alone. Also Aug 13 — the claw came out of play by your call; conventional on every length now, with the claw held as the reserve.

AUG 30 2026 — labelling, under the new standing rule that a section must say whether it is yours or the textbook's. THE FACE was the real fix: its summary line and opening sentence asserted 'barely open is square' flatly, which is the one claim in this plan that is neither textbook nor measured — it is Jack's own read, and the section's later paragraphs already hedged it while the collapsed card did not. Now split into what standard practice says (aim square), what he found (aim barely open to GET square), and why those are not in conflict. THE REHEARSALS' posture-transfer claim is now flagged as reasoned rather than sourced. No instruction changed.

briefing.focus: Everything past about six feet. Build this putter's power curve with numbers: the ladder twice a week, three numbers logged every time, the 20/30/40 backstroke map, and the tape test whose full protocol is in here. Conventional grip and full stroke length. Since Sep 10 the grip is a real split rather than a formality — the claw is the short-putt grip now — so conventional past six feet is an instruction on this card, not just the default. The pop stroke belongs to the Short Putts plan and must not come out here either.
rules: PAST ~6 FEET — CONVENTIONAL grip, full stroke length, no pop. The claw stops at six
Pace is the open fault — the ladder IS the grind
10 from 30 ft, twice a week: log SHORTS · SPREAD · GREEN SPEED
Distance = stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo — 2.0:1 is already right
Run the TAPE TEST — strike is a distance fault before it is a line fault
NO forward press (Aug 25) — the trigger is a RE-GRIP, so nothing leans the shaft at all
Gamer ball only · conventional grip · the trail hand is the FEEL hand out here and only out here

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance.

SPREAD — front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control and the number that shows improvement. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). Not optional: a stroke that finishes perfectly on an 8–9 runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11, so build the curve on at least TWO speeds before trusting it.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — a landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is the curve.

sections.t: Where distance comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
The ingredient most people are missing, you have: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. So the discipline in every ladder session is: same tempo, always — count it, hum it, whatever keeps it stable — and change the LENGTH.

The failure mode is the reverse: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself — note it on the sheet.

Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark, everything between them is interpolation, and lag putting becomes a reference you consult instead of a feeling you summon.

sections.t: Strike — the hidden speed leak
sections.k: Off-centre contact bleeds ball speed. Twelve minutes of foot powder before any verdict on this putter.
sections.b:
A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss moves. A heel strike also rotates the face closed. One cause, both faults, and it has never been measured on any putter you've owned.

This blade raises the stakes: less MOI than a mallet, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle — and its riser hosel makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. If strike is your leak, the ladder will show it as a wide spread, and the tape test will show you where it's coming from.

So run the tape test EARLY — tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 and 30 feet, with the 30-footer as the verdict. The full protocol is the next section. Use the barely-open address, since that's the setup you actually play.

sections.t: The tape test — the whole protocol, twelve minutes
sections.k: Hang it and tap it to find the true sweet spot, then two powder sheets at two distances — the 30-footer is the verdict.
sections.b:
STEP ONE — FIND THE TRUE SWEET SPOT. Hang the putter from the top of the grip so it swings free. Tap the face heel-to-toe with a pencil eraser and watch the head: everywhere off-centre it TWISTS, and at one spot it swings straight back with no twist. That spot is the true sweet spot. Mark it with a sliver of tape.

Then check the mark against the sight line. On this head the shaft is a poor pointer to where the mass sits — the riser hosel offsets it — so don't trust your eye. If the mark and the sight line disagree, that disagreement is a finding on its own: you have been lining up a spot that isn't the middle.

STEP TWO — THE POWDER SHEETS. Coat the face with foot-powder spray. Hit 10 putts from 5 feet. Photograph the face. Re-coat, hit 10 from 30 feet, photograph again. Don't wipe between putts — the overlapping marks ARE the data. Use the setup you actually play — and since Sep 10 that is TWO setups, so it is three coats rather than an optional extra. Barely-open face and hands over the head on all of them. The 30-footers are CONVENTIONAL, because that is the grip you play out there. The 5-footers are CLAW, because that is the grip you play in there. And run a conventional coat at 5 feet as well, kept separate, because comparing the two at the SAME distance is the only way the sheets can say whether the claw moved your strike — which is a real question now that the grip is decided and nobody has ever looked at it. Never let coats mix; the overlapping marks within one coat are the data, and marks from two grips on one face are noise.

HOW TO READ THEM. TIGHT CLUSTER ON THE MARK — strike isn't your leak, and pace work is pure stroke-length calibration. CLUSTER OFF-CENTRE, especially toward the HEEL — one cause explaining both open faults at once, since heel contact rotates the face closed (starts it left) and bleeds ball speed (finishes short); fixable with distance-to-ball and eyeline, not with a new putter. BROAD SCATTER — the ladder's spread has its cause, because a strike that moves is a ball speed that moves.

The 30-FOOT sheet is the one that matters — long putts are where a speed leak shows. The 5-foot sheet is the baseline that says whether the leak is stroke-length dependent. Send both photos when you run it.

sections.t: Setup for pace — four lines
sections.k: Marked ball position, vertical shaft, quiet hands, gamer ball. Pace has no other setup inputs.
sections.b:
BALL marked 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel, same spot every rep — launch is sensitive to it, and a wandering ball position reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, shaft vertical AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT — and as of Aug 25 there is nothing in front of it: the forward press is out and your trigger is a RE-GRIP, which is a pressure change rather than a position change, so it does not touch this. That is the best outcome this plan could have asked for. A lag is nothing but pace, a varying launch is a varying pace, and with nothing leaning the shaft there is nothing to vary. What DOES carry to this plan is the re-grip's own guard: land it on the same light pressure every time, because firmer hands is a quicker putt and this is the plan that pace is measured on. Its rules live in the Routine plan.

QUIET HANDS, shoulders run it.

GAMER BALL ONLY on all pace work, and CONVENTIONAL grip. That used to be the grip on every length, which made the ladder numbers and the short-putt numbers directly comparable; SINCE SEP 10 IT IS NOT, and they are NOT. The claw is the grip inside six feet, so the two sets of numbers differ by a grip as well as by a stroke length and a difference between them cannot be attributed to either. Each side of the line gets measured against itself. Nothing about this plan's own numbers changed — the ladder has always been conventional and still is — only the claim that it could be read across.

AND THE TRAIL-HAND FEEL CUE IS NOW EXCLUSIVELY YOURS OUT HERE. The right hand sensing the weight of the head is a conventional-grip cue, there is no feel hand in a claw, and there is no distance to feel inside six feet anyway. It was always a lag cue. It is now a lag cue that physically cannot leak into the short ones. What must NOT come out here is the pop stroke: a short backstroke with force added is the exact failure this plan exists to prevent.

sections.t: What the numbers are for now
sections.k: The putter is settled, so the ladder stopped being a trial and became a calibration.
sections.b:
The keep-or-return gate this section used to hold is CLOSED — you kept the LINK by decision on Aug 12 and shut the return window yourself. That changes what the numbers are for, and it is a better job than the one they had.

They are no longer evidence in a trial. Nothing on the ladder can now send a head back, which means nothing on the ladder needs defending. Two weeks of numbers at two different green speeds plus the tape test now buy you a power curve you can consult instead of a feeling you summon — and if the spread stays wide with a centred sheet, the answer is head WEIGHT or reps, not a fifth putter.

Head weight is the dial, and it is the cheapest one left. A heavier head produces a shorter, more repeatable stroke for a given distance, which usually helps lag control; a lighter head asks for a longer stroke and gives more feel on the short ones. Don't touch it before you have baseline numbers, or you will be changing two things at once and learn nothing.

And the standing rule survives everything: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: What's already settled
sections.k: Path, tempo, lift, stance — measured, closed, and none of them walked out with any putter.
sections.b:
Path: straight, SBST, confirmed across four heads. Tempo: 2.0:1 on this putter. Early lift: closed on film. Stance line: square, never open. Start line: downgraded — the one-way left pull did not reproduce across three measured putts.

What's open is pace and strike, and both are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers. The rule stands: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the work above.
sections.b:
SEP 10 2026 — the claw became the grip inside about six feet, your call, so this plan's grip line stopped being a formality and became an instruction: conventional PAST six feet. One claim was removed rather than softened — that the ladder numbers and the short-putt numbers are directly comparable because both were conventional. They are two grips now and they are not. The tape test gained a third coat so the claw's strike can be compared against conventional at the same distance.

Aug 25: the forward press came out by your decision, replaced by a late release and re-grip, so this plan's 'SAME SIZE every time' guard on the press retires — there is no press to keep the same size. The reasoning behind it does not retire and never has: a varying launch is a varying pace. It now applies to grip PRESSURE instead of shaft position, which is the one thing a re-grip can vary.

Aug 14: the forward press came back as the trigger by your call, so this plan's 'no FORWARD press' rule is retired and re-scoped like the others — vertical AT IMPACT, with the press recovering into it. The reasoning that rule carried is NOT retired and is now the guard on the press itself: a varying launch is a varying pace, and pace is the open fault on this plan.

The DF3i went back on Aug 10 for distance control — after being benched for pace Jul 30, reprieved Aug 1 and returned Aug 10: three verdicts in eleven days, all on feel, zero calibrated lag sessions. That pattern, not the putter, is what this plan exists to break. The Aug 1 'pace felt dialled' round was a scramble on 8–9 stimp greens — the friendliest read available. The Aug 10 outdoor session scored ~20 putts off above-ground cups: nine dead, worst ~4 ft, nothing long — first real evidence pace is closer than the returns implied. The blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot — hence the gamer-ball rule. Both reds on the evolution grid (face at impact, start line) were measured on this head Jul 30; the start-line red was downgraded Aug 10 pm after the mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — dispersion, no bias.

Aug 13: the Tape Test folded in from its own plan — it was always the same subject as this one, since strike is a distance fault before it is a line fault. Written Aug 2 for the DF3i, moved to the LINK Aug 10, still unrun on any of the four putters owned this month. Two Aug 10 pointers both aim at it: the evening mat putts scattered ~0.8° either side with no bias (a moving strike is the leading explanation on a head that cannot twist), and the blue ball spread 1.2-1.5 ft on putts the white killed. The keep-or-return gate closed Aug 12 when you kept the putter by decision.

briefing.focus: Every putting question worked through end to end, one per section, newest first. This is the reference shelf, not the routine — nothing here tells you what to do on a putt. Tap a section to open it; each one says what was asked, what checked out, what did not, what changed in the other plans, and what is still unmeasured.
rules: One section per workshop, NEWEST FIRST — tap to open, they stay shut otherwise
Every section says WHAT CHANGED in the other plans, so nothing here is orphaned
Sourced claims and reasoned ones are labelled differently — on purpose
This is a REFERENCE. What you actually do lives in the Routine plan

sections.t: Sep 10 2026 — The claw is the grip inside six feet, and the tour data is not a tailwind
sections.k: Your decision settles the grip and simplifies the experiment; the outside evidence says the mechanism is agreed, nobody has measured the result, and the one tour dataset available points the other way for reasons that are probably selection.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. On Sep 10 you said: "Claw grip from now on for short putts. Maybe 6ft and less." That is an intent, so it is authoritative and it is the instruction from today. What was worth working through is everything downstream of it — what it does to the experiment that was running, what standard practice actually claims for it, and what the evidence is.

WHAT YOU SAID. The claw, every short putt, six feet and less. The hedge in "maybe" is on the BOUNDARY, not on the grip.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS. The mechanism is not in dispute and it is taught the same way everywhere: the trail hand comes off the handle and pinches the grip from the side, which moves pressure into the lead hand, gives the trail hand a passive guiding role, and makes a wrist flip physically awkward. The stated benefit is stopping the trail hand hitting at the putt — the yip case. The stated COST is distance control, and it is stated by essentially everyone who teaches it: with no hand releasing, judging speed is harder, and it is reported as hardest on long putts and on slow greens. That is the same trade this project already had written down (a little distance feel for line control), arrived at independently, and it checks out.

WHERE STANDARD PRACTICE AND YOUR PLAN AGREE EXACTLY, and this is the useful confirmation: the textbook cost of the claw lands on LONG putts and SLOW greens. Your greens are estimated 8-9 stimp — slow — and pace is your open fault. So the six-foot quarantine this plan has drawn since Aug 13, which was reasoned from your own situation rather than from any source, is exactly where the outside advice would put it too. The boundary is not arbitrary and it is now corroborated.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — and it is worth reading properly rather than as a warning. There is no controlled study showing the claw makes more putts. Searched for one; what exists is instruction and one cross-sectional tour analysis. GOLF DIGEST analysed the top 125 players of the 2022-23 FedEx Cup season through the Tour Championship across the five most common putting methods: cross-handed users (24 players) averaged the best strokes-gained/putting rank at 69, the standard grip came second at 75.2, and CLAW USERS AVERAGED THE WORST RANK FROM FOUR TO EIGHT FEET, with only one of them (Taylor Pendrith) inside the top 20 at that range. Four to eight feet is very nearly the range you have just adopted it for.

WHY THAT IS NOT THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IT THAT IT LOOKS LIKE. It is cross-sectional, not a trial, and the selection runs the wrong way in the most obvious manner possible: players adopt the claw BECAUSE their short putting has gone, not at random. A grip taken up by the tour's worst short putters will show up as the grip with the worst short putters on it whether it helps them or not — you would need their numbers BEFORE the switch to say anything, and the analysis does not have them. So the honest reading is that this dataset cannot tell you whether the claw works; it can only tell you that the population using it is not a flattering one. What it does establish is that there is no measured tailwind here — nobody can hand you evidence that this will hole more putts.

PROVENANCE ON THAT FIGURE: the Golf Digest article itself could not be opened from this session (the domain is blocked at the network layer), so the season, the player counts and the two rank averages come from search snippets of it and an Australian Golf Digest reprint, and the number of claw users in the sample is NOT KNOWN. Treat the 69 and the 75.2 as reported-but-unverified. The 4-8 ft claim is the one being leaned on and it is the one stated most consistently across the snippets.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE OTHER PLANS. SHORT PUTTS — INSIDE SIX FEET is the one that actually moved. The four-combination test order (baseline / pop only / claw only / both) collapsed to TWO blocks, both claw, differing only in the stroke — a better experiment than the one it replaced, because the grip dial is now nailed down instead of being something to work around. The old conventional-grip baseline retired with it, including Jul 20's 8/10 from four feet, so that plan currently has no scoreboard at all until the first claw block gets run. The LOFT TRAP went from one suspect back to two: a claw can push the handle forward without the hands reporting it, where the pop leans the shaft in a way you might feel. GRIP & POSTURE lost its 'CONVENTIONAL, BOTH LENGTHS' rule and the claw's reserve framing. The ROUTINE plan's note that began 'IF THE CLAW EVER COMES BACK OFF THE SHELF' became a live check — the re-grip trigger now lands in two different grips depending on the length of the putt, and its dwell count is two numbers now. LAG PUTTS lost a claim outright rather than having it softened: that the ladder numbers and the short-putt numbers are directly comparable because both were conventional. They are two grips now and they are not.

THE ONE NEW RULE THAT CAME OUT OF IT. "About six feet" is a judgment made standing over the ball, so it needed a tie-breaker: IF YOU ARE UNSURE WHICH SIDE OF SIX YOU ARE ON, IT IS A LAG — conventional. The asymmetry is real and one-directional. A claw on a putt that turns out to be long spends a distance-feel trade on the exact shot where pace is the open fault; conventional on a putt that turns out to be short means you held it the way you have held it all year. Only one of those two errors lands on the thing being measured.

STILL UNMEASURED, and the list got longer rather than shorter. No claw rep has ever been filmed or scored on this putter, or on any putter in this project — the Grip Experiment's 'claw shelved' verdict was reached in July on the DF3i, with the Press Pistol 2° and the left miss still live, and all three of those have since changed, so it never bound anything. The 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK on either grip. The face-on clip is owed TWICE now, once per grip, because comparing address to impact is the only thing that can catch a claw creeping the handle forward on a 2° face. And the tape test gained a third coat: conventional at 30 ft, claw at 5 ft, conventional at 5 ft, kept separate, because a same-distance comparison is the only way the sheets can say whether the new grip moved your strike.

THE HONEST SUMMARY. The grip is decided and that is not up for measurement. What the measurement is for now is different and narrower: to find out what the claw is worth, so that everything after it has something to be compared against. Right now this project cannot say whether the claw helps you, and the outside world cannot say either.

SOURCES. Mechanism and stated costs: Golf Monthly (Alex Elliott), Today's Golfer, GolfLink, HoleThePutt — consistent across all of them, which is why the mechanism is treated as agreed rather than as any one source's claim. Tour data: Golf Digest, 'Which putting grip performs best on the PGA Tour? We analyzed the stats', 2022-23 FedEx Cup season, top 125 through the Tour Championship — via search snippets only, domain blocked. Searched for and did not find: any controlled or peer-reviewed study of claw versus conventional putting performance. The EMG literature that turns up on this search is about GRIP SIZE in the full swing and does not transfer.

sections.t: Aug 27 2026 — Outside at last, the camera in the right place, and the sun took the ball away
sections.k: The first putting film on a real green with the camera down the target line — and clipped exposure made the ball and the turf the same pixel, which cost every measurement the angle was chosen for.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Every capture note for a month said the same three things: get off the mat, get the camera onto the target line, and stop measuring a room. This session did all three. Did it deliver?

WHAT CHECKED OUT. The capture itself, on every axis except one. Original file, 119.5 fps, no declared slow motion and no ramp — the first putting clip in weeks whose time base can simply be believed, after two in three days that lied about theirs. Camera static to 1.13 px. Lens reads 1x, no barrel bowing on the green's mow lines. And the camera family is confirmed by measurement rather than by eye: at address the putter head OCCLUDES the ball's lower edge, so the ball is on the far side and the strike sends it away from the lens; and through the stroke the head travels 4 px laterally against 18 px in depth, which is a stroke running along the camera axis. Scale is 35.7 px per inch at the ball, from the ball's own 1.68 inches, cross-checked against the putter head reading 5.2 inches — right for a LINK.2.1 blade, and an independent object.

WHAT DID NOT — AND IT IS ONE THING, WHICH IS THE GOOD NEWS. Direct midday sun on a light green clipped the sensor. The ball measures BGR 141/248/245 at address; the grass six inches away measures 159/249/244. Green and blue are both railed at 248–255 across the entire frame, so the ball and the turf are the same pixel values and only blue carries any separation, inside the noise floor. Four tracking methods were tried and failed in four different ways — a brightness threshold locked onto shoes and the flagstick, a local median subtraction lost the ball to its own background, a saturation gate found it sitting inside the grass distribution, and motion mode locked onto wind in the treeline and walkers on the horizon. Start line, green break, roll-out and ball speed — the four things this camera position was chosen to get — all died there. A clipped sensor does not degrade gracefully; it rails a whole channel at its maximum, so two objects of genuinely different brightness come back identical. A white ball on a bright green is the worst case for it, and it is the exact pairing every putting measurement depends on.

THE REJECTED NUMBER. This clip produced a tempo of 0.95:1 and it is rejected for a structural reason, not for noise. A down-the-line camera foreshortens the stroke along the depth axis, so at the start of the backswing the head is moving slowly AND its motion is compressed — onset falls under the detection floor and gets picked up late, which shortens the measured backswing while leaving the fast through-stroke about right. The bias runs one way: this camera family UNDER-REPORTS the ratio. 0.95:1 against a 2:1 target is a projection artifact, not a fault.

That settles something useful about the standing argument, though: a ratio measured down the line is NOT POOLABLE with one measured face-on. The app's 2.0:1 at n=8 and the pipeline's 1.79:1 at n=6 are both face-on and remain the only two live numbers. This session is not a third sample.

A SIGN CONVENTION THAT INVERTS, and it is the trap worth carrying forward. Every session on file says 'image-right = Jack's left'. True for a camera at the HOLE END. From BEHIND the ball it is backwards — image-right is Jack's RIGHT, because he stands image-left of the ball with the target running away from the lens, so image left-to-right crosses his stance instead of running along the line. Any number read off a behind-the-ball clip using the target-end convention has its sign flipped. WHICH RAISES A QUESTION about the three Aug 10 start lines: that evening was shot from BOTH angles and the record never says which clips produced 0.8° right, 1.0° left and 0.6° right. Worth asking the pipeline to confirm. The conclusion drawn from them does not move either way — a mean bias of about 0.1° is zero whichever sign it carries — but the individual numbers would.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE REPORT. It calls this camera family a first for the project. It is a first for the ANALYSIS PIPELINE, which is what it actually claims — but this app already holds behind-the-ball down-the-line film from Aug 10 (img0015/0016/0017), and that is where the three start-line numbers came from. What is genuinely new is the angle OUTDOORS, on grass.

AND THE MAT NUMBERS STAY ON THE MAT. The ~4.9 inch break with a flat first 42 inches is a property of that mat's setup and transfers to a bentgrass green not at all. Whatever this green does was not measured. No make count exists either, and none could: he was aimed at a pin with no hole cut, so nothing could go in.

WHAT CHANGED. The camera-prep action opens with the exposure rule now: expose for the BALL, not the scene — tap it before recording, or lock down a stop or two, or shoot with the sun lower. A yellow or orange ball fixes it outright and is the cheapest version by a distance. Second addition: don't shoot tempo from down the line at all. Tempo wants face-on, start line wants down-the-line, and if both are wanted they are two setups rather than one.

STILL UNMEASURED, and the split is finally clean, which it has never been before. On EXPOSURE, one tap away: start line in degrees, green break, roll-out, ball speed, pace. On FRAME RATE, because 119.5 does not reach the 240 floor: face angle at impact, strike location, low point, attack angle. On CAMERA POSITION: absolute path and SBST retrace want an overhead; tempo wants face-on. Also unestablished: how many putts are actually in the clip. At least six address-and-stroke episodes are visible, but without a trackable ball there is no strike marker, so nothing separates a stroke from a practice stroke.

WORTH NAMING, because it is new. Aug 25 chipping was blocked on surface and frame rate; Aug 26's re-read was blocked on camera position; this one is blocked on exposure. Three sessions, three different blockers, each characterised and each cheaper than the last. Nothing here is a repeat failure — the first time that has been true since the filming started.

SOURCES. '2026-08-27 — Outdoor green, down-the-line capture, exposure blocker', Drive, Putting/Analysis Reports. Camera family and the exposure clipping [VERIFIED]; scale [DERIVED]; session inventory [OBSERVED, moderate confidence]; tempo REJECTED by the report itself. The correction on 'a first for this project', and the Aug 10 sign-convention question, were raised here against the existing record.

sections.t: Aug 26 2026 — The Aug 10 mat film re-read at 240 fps: a missing clip, a lying time base, and the blocker changes
sections.k: Two stroke durations measured to a single frame, a fourth evening clip nobody had logged — and the reason the face is still unmeasured stops being frame rate and becomes camera position.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. The Aug 10 evening mat film was shot down the target line and read once, in August, for start line. Could a proper re-analysis at full frame rate pull anything more out of footage already on file — and does any of it change what is standing?

WHAT CHECKED OUT. Four things, and the first one is not a measurement at all.

A CLIP NOBODY HAD LOGGED. IMG_3475 sits immediately before the three hole-end clips that are in the record, from the same target-end position, and carries TWO putts with the camera falling over between them. The evening set was written down as “6 clips, COMPLETE · 3 putts.” It was not complete. Whether those two putts are additional to the logged three or a spoiled take later re-shot as 3476–3478 cannot be settled from the footage, so the start-line set now reads as three measured putts out of at least five attempted. That is a small correction with a real edge on it: the open fault on this page is SCATTER, and a scatter number computed over three putts when five were struck is the wrong denominator.

TWO DOWNSTROKES, TO A SINGLE FRAME. 0.200 s and 0.221 s — impact pinned on one identified frame each, both balls sitting still to ±0.15 px for hundreds of frames beforehand. At 240 fps that is 4 ms of resolution, and they are the first absolute stroke durations in this project that are measured rather than inferred. Brisk against the 0.23–0.30 s of Sessions 4 and 5, but inside his own range, and 10% apart from each other.

THE MAT BREAK, CORROBORATED WITHOUT A RULER. Each ball's drift from its own initial-roll line, scaled by its own 1.68-inch diameter so no focal length is needed: +0.14 in and +0.18 in, both to Jack's LEFT, on two different camera positions with two independently fitted reference lines. Small, and it should be — the sampled stretch is the early flat part of the roll, which is exactly where the ~4.9-inch-at-the-hole result says the trace is flat. Direction corroborated; no new number.

AND THE TRACKED OBJECT IS THE HEAD. 4.5 inches wide at address against the ball as ruler, against a LINK.2.1 blade of 4.3–4.6. Previously assumed.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT, and the analysis said so itself rather than being caught. Two numbers came back rejected and are written here so they cannot be rediscovered later and believed. FIRST, a whole depth chain — 9.2 ft/s ball speed, 107 inches of roll, a 10.2 ft address distance — all computed on an assumed 1x lens, and all wrong. The giveaway was a fitted deceleration of MINUS 4.5 ft/s²: the ball reading as accelerating down the mat, which cannot happen. Cause: as the ball nears the lens it brightens and blurs, more pixels clear the threshold, and measured diameter inflates faster than 1/Z, so every depth-derived quantity inherits the bias. SECOND, a half-cosine extrapolation invented to recover the unseen takeaway onset. On one putt it returned an answer below its own hard acquisition bound — arithmetically impossible — so it cannot be trusted on the other either. That is why the tempo ratios stand as bounds.

THE FILE LIED ABOUT ITS TIME BASE, for the second time in two days. IMG_3475 presents a flat 30 fps over 7,327 frames and 244 seconds, no ramp anywhere. It is a 240 fps capture baked 8x slow, so true elapsed is 30.5 seconds and every duration read off its own timestamps is eight times too long. Three container facts corroborate the slowing independently of Jack's word — playback-intent flag at 0, audio 84% below 200 Hz (time-stretched, not a live room), and motion energy flat across thousands of frames with no burst at either stroke. THE FACTOR OF 8 rests on Jack saying he shot 240, which is his to state. The internal check that supports it: at 120 fps the two downstrokes would be 0.40 and 0.44 s, which is implausibly slow for a putt. No conflict with the rest of the record — the 120 fps note on that day belongs to the afternoon batch of 23, and the evening mat clips never had a frame rate written down at all.

One consequence worth stating because it is easy to get backwards: a RATIO is scale-free, so the 8x error does not touch a single tempo number anywhere in this project. It touches absolute durations only.

WHAT CHANGED. The camera-prep action is re-ranked and now opens with the finding rather than the checklist: FRAME RATE IS NO LONGER THE BLOCKER, CAMERA POSITION IS. That is the most useful thing to come out of this read. The standing story for five weeks was that 30 fps gave six to nine frames through the forward stroke and nothing could be pulled from it; this clip proves the frame rate is available and impact can be pinned to 4 ms — and face angle, strike location, shaft lean and early lift are all still unmeasured anyway. They are blocked on WHERE THE PHONE SAT. A lens 9–12 inches off the floor sees the face edge-on and the shaft from below; and from straight down the target line, head HEIGHT and head DEPTH project onto the same image row, which makes early lift degenerate rather than merely hard. Different problem, cheaper to fix. The evolution grid's Tempo row also moves from a dash to a partial in the Aug 10 mat column. And a stale gear reference was corrected while in there — the action still described the LINK's grip as a Pistol 0, which was fixed on Aug 14.

STILL UNMEASURED. Face angle at impact, strike location, shaft lean at impact, early lift, absolute arc — all capture, all camera position now rather than frame rate. Absolute distances, speeds and angles: the lens is unidentified, a barrel-distortion test on the mat rails came back self-contradictory (34 px of implied sagitta on one rail against 3 px on the other) and is void, and the depth chain that might have identified the lens is the one that was rejected. Two balls exactly 12 inches apart in frame, once per session, collapses that permanently — and it cannot be applied retroactively to anything already shot. The tempo conflict is untouched: 2.0:1 at n=8, 1.79:1 at n=6, and now bounds of ≥1.90 and ≥1.51 at n=2. None arbitrates the others, and it remains Jack's call.

ONE THING IS RECOVERABLE WITHOUT FILMING ANYTHING. Start line relative to the mat failed here only because the centre-line detector locked onto the mat's solid rails instead of its dashed line (RMS 63 px). That is a processing problem, not a capture one, and it is fixable on this same footage — which would add two more start-line measurements to a set of three, on the open scatter question, from a camera position that suits the measurement. Worth asking for.

SOURCES. “2026-08-26 — Putting re-analysis, IMG_3475 (Aug 10 LINK.2.1, 240fps) — both putts”, Drive, Putting/Analysis Reports. An earlier same-day file of nearly the same name covered putt 1 only and was withdrawn by its successor; it was deliberately not read, to avoid re-importing a number the newer file had corrected. Tags as given: the time base [VERIFIED], impact frames, downstrokes, tempo bounds and mat drift all [DERIVED], each with n and method.

sections.t: Aug 24 2026 — Ten clips: the break gets a number, SBST is confirmed twice, and a settled fault nearly came back on a motion-blur artifact
sections.k: Every miss is LEFT and it is still an under-read break; SBST now has two unrelated methods agreeing; tempo runs quick across six strokes; and the early-lift challenge inverted under replication, which is the part worth reading.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Ten clips in one day: seven putts on the PuttOut AirBreak across two batches on one untouched tilt, and three stroke clips on the strip mat with the phone flat behind the ball. What do they establish, and what did three separate passes over them get wrong?

THE MAT, AND IT IS SETTLED IN SHAPE. Every putt in both AirBreak batches bends to his LEFT. Deviation from each ball's own start line grows as the SQUARE of distance rolled, and across the four measured putts the break is monotonic in pace with no exceptions: 95% of speed retained broke 2.54 in, 87% broke 2.87, 84% broke 3.53, 80% broke 3.95. A ball started off-line travels a straight line and its offset grows LINEARLY; these do not. That test needs no scale and no centre-line assumption either, because straightness survives projection — run on raw pixels the four curvature coefficients land on top of each other, and a fifth putt tracked separately came in at 2.59e-4, inside the same band.

THE SENTENCE TO KEEP: THE MISS IS THE ONE THAT STARTED AT THE TARGET. The mat wants roughly 2.5° of right start line at this pace. The putt that gave it 0.10° finished 4 in left; the three that allowed 1.6–2.9° all went in. Across both batches four holed and three missed, and every miss went LEFT — which on a surface falling left is an under-read break, not the aim fault this project has chased since July.

A CORRECTION THAT STRENGTHENS IT. The write-up of the second putt said it "never moves right at all, left from the first frame." Tracked properly over 366 points that is wrong: its lateral offset is FLAT at +1.37 to +1.40 in for the first 42 inches of roll and only then accelerates. A start-line error produces linear drift from the first inch and there is none. Measured start line −0.29° against the mat axis. The whole leftward movement is accumulated break.

SBST, CONFIRMED BY A SECOND AND UNRELATED METHOD. This is the strongest result of the day. For a head at depth Z the image gives lateral position as (x − principal point)/W and depth as 1/W, where W is the head's apparent width — so a STRAIGHT line in three dimensions makes the first linear in the second, whatever the focal length and whatever the head's real size. On two stroke clips the residuals come back under 1% of the head's own lateral excursion, back and through, with the two directions fitting slopes within 2% of each other. The head retraces its own line. No loop, no arc.

Re-running it here found the one assumption that was not named: the test is free of focal length and head size but NOT of the PRINCIPAL POINT, and sweeping that across a plausible range moves the residual from about 3% to about 9% and the back-versus-through agreement from 17% to 42%. On top of that, the geometry only reconciles at a focal length near 700–780 px, i.e. the 0.5x ultra-wide — and barrel distortion bends straight lines, which is exactly what a straightness test measures. So: confirmed in SHAPE, from a genuinely independent camera and method, with the sub-1% precision read as softer than quoted. Given SBST was already settled across 20+ clips and four putters from overhead, that is the right weight.

TEMPO RUNS QUICK, AND THE METHOD MIGHT BE WHY. Two stroke clips give 1.71:1 and 1.56:1. Pooled with the four AirBreak strokes — 1.64, 1.82, 1.86, 2.13 — that is SIX STROKES across two sessions, two mats and two camera positions, mean about 1.79, five of six under 2:1. Jul 30 had 7 of 8 clips landing 1.9–2.1. The direction is consistent enough to be a finding. The number is not, and the reason biases one way: backswing START is detected in both analyses as a departure from a plateau, which is threshold-sensitive and clips the slow first inches of the takeaway, SHORTENING the ratio. One hand-checked stroke calibrates the method against Jul 30's and settles it. If it is real, the mechanism is a short backswing rather than a fast downswing — the down-stroke durations cluster tightly and the backswings do not.

THE EARLY-LIFT CHALLENGE, AND WHY IT DID NOT SURVIVE. This is the part to read, because a fault closed on 120 fps film nearly reopened on it.

The method is a good one. Compare the head at MATCHED APPARENT WIDTH: both passes are then at the same depth, the mat's convex profile cancels, and no scale enters, so any difference in the sole's image row is real height. Done that way it reported the head coming through HIGHER than it went back — 3.6 px near the top, rising to 19.5 px and 29.6 px approaching the ball, or 0.3 to 0.5 inches. That is the exact shape early lift has: symmetric at the top, diverging toward the ball. And even its low end is several times the 0.05–0.08 in Jul 30 measured.

Two checks were run against it. The FIRST supports it: address sits at a head width of 224 px and the top of the backswing at 365, so the 220–226 px bucket where the effect is largest really is at ball depth, not somewhere in the follow-through. The bucketing was sound.

The SECOND kills it. An independent replication using a background-difference mask instead of a darkness threshold returns the OPPOSITE SIGN at every matched depth — the head reads 2 to 19 px LOWER coming through, not higher. And why the two disagree is measurable rather than argued: at matched depth the downswing silhouette carries 5 to 18% fewer core-dark pixels than the backswing, the deficit is LARGEST NEAR IMPACT, and the soft-edge fraction there jumps from 0.26 to 0.42. The head is about 1.7 times faster through the same depths on the way down — 72 frames back against 42 down — so it is more motion-blurred exactly where the claimed lift is biggest. A threshold that EXCLUDES the blur halo eats the smeared bottom edge and raises the apparent sole; one that INCLUDES it extends the blob downward and lowers it. Two methods, opposite signs, each in the direction its own bias predicts. That is what a measurement dominated by artifact looks like.

Early lift stays CLOSED. This is written down rather than dropped because the next reader will find the same apparent effect on the same footage, and the record should say it was chased and why it failed.

THE PATTERN IN THE DAY'S MISTAKES, worth naming. Three sweeping claims were made about this footage and all three were too broad. "The ball-height clips measure nothing" — they carry the best path measurement in the project. "This mat cannot score a start line" — it scores the line to about ±0.3°, just not the intent behind it. "Nothing in the batch can see path" — true of the target-end camera, false of the ball-height one, which is a different instrument with fifteen times the resolution on the head. The common error each time was generalising from one camera to a day's footage.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE OTHER PLANS. No stroke instruction moved. The day's session entry was widened again in place rather than duplicated. The evolution grid's Aug 24 column moved Path to a tick and Early lift to a question mark, with both verdicts rewritten. Strike location gained the first thing in the record that points at it rather than inferring it. And the delivery fault gained the reshoot spec.

THE STROKE-CLIP RESHOOT, four fixes, none of which cost anything: name the LENS or force 1x; put TWO BALLS EXACTLY 12 INCHES APART in frame before starting, so there is a scale; move the LIGHT so the head's shadow does not fall toward the lens, since at address the silhouette merges with its own shadow and the baseline goes soft by 20–30 px; and shoot at the HIGHEST FRAME RATE the phone offers, because the whole early-lift argument came apart on motion blur.

TWO LOOSE ENDS. An indirect route to face angle — ball start line minus head path — returned 0.30° and 0.80° on the two clips, which do not agree well enough to publish while the focal length is unknown. And a flag on pooling was raised and closed the same day: a shirt-colour difference between the two AirBreak batches was read off the film as evidence of two separate sessions, which would have broken the seven-putt sample apart. He changed shirts. It is all one day, one mat, one untouched tilt, and the pooling stands. Kept here as a worked example of a rule this project already has rather than as a resolved annoyance: film is king on POSITIONS and SENSATIONS, and it is not king on what he did — intent and actions are his to state, and an inference drawn from a frame does not outrank them. The correct move was to ask, and asking cost one line.

NOT MEASURED: face angle at impact; strike location; shaft lean at impact; the mat's tilt in degrees; stroke path in real angular terms, as opposed to its straightness; sole height, now actively unresolved rather than merely unmeasured; and the 30-ft ladder, still unrun. n=7 putts, n=2 stroke clips, n=6 strokes for tempo.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The loft is confirmed at 2°, and the grip was never a Pistol 0
sections.k: Two of the three specs flagged as guesses got settled off L.A.B.'s own page and a look at the putter — the loft estimate was right, the grip name was wrong, and neither one changes an instruction.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Aug 12 flagged three specs this project had been treating as fact without a source — loft, as-built length, head weight — and one contradiction: the app named an L.A.B. Pistol 0 grip while retailers listed a Lamkin Deep Etched, left as something to go and look at. Two of the four got answered on Aug 14, off L.A.B.'s own LINK.2.1 custom build page and a direct look at the putter.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — THE LOFT. L.A.B. publish it in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the custom page: EFFECTIVE LOFT: 2 DEGREES. The 2° this app has carried since Jul 30 was right.

Be precise about what that vindicates. The Aug 12 audit was still correct to flag it — at the time the number had no locatable source, and a claim whose source cannot be found is folklore whether or not it happens to be true. What was wrong was the SEARCH, not the scepticism: the figure sits in a collapsed accordion on the CUSTOM page, and every search on Aug 12 went at the stock page and the retailers. The lesson is where to look, not to trust an unsourced number next time.

Three plans were hedging that figure — how much a press de-lofts, whether hands ahead drives the ball, what '0° lean delivered' actually delivers. They can stop hedging.

THE SAME PANEL, THREE MORE FACTS. 303 stainless head, black PVD finish. Lengths 28–38" (shaft dependent). Lie angles 65–74°. That last one partly answers an Aug 12 sub-question: 70° was orderable, so 69° as-built was not L.A.B. reaching for the nearest available station. Whether it was a deliberate build choice or a tolerance outcome against the 70° target is still unanswered — and still irrelevant, at 0.035° of face aim.

WHAT DID NOT — THE GRIP. It is a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED, confirmed by looking at the putter. The app said L.A.B. Pistol 0 from Jul 30 to Aug 14, written down as 'stock spec confirmed by research'. Fifteen days wrong.

NOTHING DOWNSTREAM CHANGES, and it is worth saying WHY rather than just asserting it. Every use of that name in this project was a stand-in for exactly one property: zero built-in lean. The Lamkin Deep Etched has zero built-in lean too. So the geometry the plans describe — shaft vertical, hands about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, the DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue dead and never to be carried across — is untouched. And it was never resting on the label in the first place: Jul 30 film measured the shaft dead vertical and repeatable to 0.3° across 59 frames. Film is king, and here the film was right while the label was wrong — which is the cleanest demonstration of that rule this project has produced.

WHAT CHANGED IN THE PLANS. The bag spec and a dated history row carry the corrected grip and the confirmed loft. GRIP & POSTURE and SWING THOUGHTS both named the Pistol 0 and now don't — text only, no instruction moved. The saga section of this log keeps its original wording with a SINCE UPDATED line appended, because a log records what was believed at the time.

STILL UNMEASURED — and these two matter more than the loft did. AS-BUILT LENGTH: 34" was targeted and has never been confirmed, and it is the denominator in the handle-height number (1" of hand lift = 1.7° at 34", roughly fifty times the lie tolerance). HEAD WEIGHT: never known on any of the four putters owned this month, and the most direct lever there is on distance control, which is the open fault. Neither is a catalogue fact. That is precisely why a product page could settle the loft and cannot settle these — they are build-order facts, and they need L.A.B. support or a shop with a scale.

SOURCES. RESEARCHED — labgolf.com, LINK.2.1 custom putter page, SPECIFICATIONS panel: loft, head material, finish, length range, lie range; read Aug 14 2026. OBSERVED — the grip, by looking at the putter.

sections.t: Aug 14 — THE FORWARD PRESS, BACK BY DECISION
sections.k: The press is yours again by choice; it is only compatible with this putter if it RECOVERS, and that it recovers is unmeasured.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack: "I'm gonna go with the forward press for putting trigger again — feels the best of them all, before the takeaway." He had run the shelf of triggers from the Aug 13 workshop and picked one. Which trigger he runs is his call and is not overridable by film; whether it costs him anything is not.

WHAT IT COLLIDED WITH. Three live rules said the opposite, in three different plans: GRIP & POSTURE's "NO FORWARD PRESS. Shaft VERTICAL at address and VERTICAL at impact"; the ROUTINE plan's "FORWARD PRESS stays out permanently"; and SHORT PUTTS' "SHAFT STILL VERTICAL — a rap that leans forward delofts a face with little to give." Leaving any of those standing would have left two live sources for one instruction, so all three were changed in the same pass.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — the distinction that resolves it. A forward press is two different moves sharing a name. A press that RECOVERS is a trigger: the hands go forward, the shaft returns to vertical as the stroke starts, and the ball is struck with zero lean. A press that is HELD — where the stroke begins from the pressed position — leaves the shaft leaning at impact, which delofts and drives the ball into the turf. Jack described a trigger run BEFORE the takeaway, which is the recovering kind, and that version conflicts with nothing the film has established. So the rule did not have to be abandoned, only re-scoped: the vertical-shaft requirement was always really about IMPACT, and 'vertical at address' was a proxy for it that only held while nothing moved.

WHAT DID NOT CHECK OUT — the ban's own footing. The Aug 10 removal was not measured either. It rested on two things: the deloft arithmetic, which this project already corrected on Aug 13 when it found that the ~2° of loft is an ESTIMATE (no retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a figure for this head), and the observation that a VARYING press is a varying pace. The second one survives intact and is the strongest guard on the new trigger; the first is directional rather than exact. So this is not film being overturned by feel — it is one unfilmed preference replacing another, which is worth stating plainly.

WHAT CHANGED ELSEWHERE. ROUTINE: the trigger rule, the trigger section and step 6 now name the forward press, and the trail-thumb press is out (one trigger, never two). GRIP & POSTURE: the NO FORWARD PRESS rule is retired and THE SHAFT section re-scoped to impact. SHORT PUTTS: same re-scope, plus a new warning that press-plus-pop is the highest-risk pairing on the card — a short firm rap is the stroke with the least time to give the lean back, so if a scuff shows up anywhere it shows up inside six feet first.

WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED. That the press recovers at all — nobody has filmed it. The size of the press, which has no number on it and will drift exactly the way 'barely open' has drifted for weeks. Whether it changes pace, which matters more than usual because PACE CALIBRATION is the open fault and a leaked lean finishes putts SHORT. Two detectors already exist and neither needs new equipment: the face-on clip (shaft angle at address, at the top of the press, and at impact — matching address and impact is the pass) and the 30-ft ladder that is already the standing work, where a press leaking lean shows up as shorts that were not there before.

SOURCES. Jack's own decision, Aug 14, reported as a feel ('feels the best of them all'). Everything else here is prior project record: the Aug 10 press removal and the Press Pistol 2° that left with the DF3i; the Aug 13 loft-estimate correction; the Jul 30 film establishing a vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°; and the open pace fault. No new measurement was taken today.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 14, later the same day): this section leans on the loft being an ESTIMATE when it weighs the old ban's footing. It was confirmed at 2° hours afterwards — L.A.B. publishes 2° effective loft for this head in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the LINK.2.1 custom build page — confirmed Aug 14, so this is a spec now, not an inference. The estimate turned out to be correct, so the reasoning above is unaffected: the ban rested on arithmetic that is now sourced rather than inferred, and the decision to run a press that RECOVERS is the same decision either way. What changes is that 'the margin is not measured' is no longer true, and the ROUTINE and SHORT PUTTS plans were updated to stop saying it.

SINCE UPDATED (Aug 25 2026): the press is OUT again, by Jack's decision — "I kinda just do late release and regrab with my hands right now but no forward press." This section's finding stands exactly as written and is not edited: the recovering-versus-held distinction is still the right analysis of a forward press, and it is still what would make one safe on this head. What has changed is that there is no longer a press to apply it to. Three consequences. The vertical-shaft rule reverted from IMPACT to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT across the ROUTINE, GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS plans — the same four that were changed in one pass on Aug 14, changed in one pass again. The 'WHAT IS STILL UNMEASURED' list above is now moot rather than answered: nobody ever did film whether the press recovered, and nobody now will, so the owed clip closed by decision and not by evidence. And the new trigger relocates the risk rather than removing it — a re-grip cannot lean the shaft, but it CAN land on a firmer grip pressure than the one it let go of, which is the main way a trail hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one. That guard now lives in GRIP & POSTURE, where pressure lives. Worth stating plainly, since this section made the same point about its predecessor: this is the third trigger in fifteen days and the third adopted on feel with nothing filmed. Which trigger he runs is his call and always was. That none of the three has ever been measured is the finding. LATER THE SAME DAY: the re-grip was made a DELIBERATE trigger rather than a noticed habit, Jack's call, held provisionally ('for now'). That does not change anything above, but it does close the one thing this section keeps flagging. A trigger's single job is shortening the dwell over the ball, and a deliberate trigger can be graded on it — ten putts timed from the last look at the hole to the takeaway, re-counted a fortnight later. It went on the trigger to-do. Three triggers in fifteen days and none of them measured; this is the first with any number owed against it, and it needs no camera, which is the reason to expect this one to actually get taken.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The pre-LINK film was deleted. Everything it measured is here.
sections.k: Eight putting sessions on three putters you no longer play were cleared out — this section keeps every number they produced, because two of them still underpin decisions you are living with.
sections.b:
WHAT HAPPENED. Jack cleared the film room of every putting session shot on a putter that is not the LINK.2.1 — the Phantom 7.5, the Newport 2 and the DF3i. Eight sessions, Jul 17 through Jul 21. His call and a reasonable one: he plays one putter now and frame-by-frame breakdowns of retired gear are not what the film room is for.

WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS ANYWAY. Two of those sessions are still load-bearing. The conclusions live on in the evolution grid, the faults and the plans, but the EVIDENCE lived only on the rows that were deleted, and a claim whose source has been thrown away quietly becomes folklore. So the numbers are written out here in full.

THE TWO THAT MATTER MOST.

(1) THE SBST CONFIRMATION — the reason you play a zero-torque putter at all. Jul 18, 9 clips overhead + down-the-line: path confirmed STRAIGHT, straight-back-straight-through. Same day, 5 more overhead clips across 3× Phantom 7.5 and 2× Newport 2: path straight on BOTH putters, face square through impact, no visible toe-over, balls starting dead on the centre line. That is the finding the whole equipment case was built on — an arc-balanced head fights a straight stroke — and it was measured on the two arc putters, which is precisely what made it convincing. It has never been re-run on the LINK because it has never needed to be.

(2) 8 OUT OF 10 FROM FOUR FEET — Jul 20, DF3i, conventional grip, 10 balls on the return mat. All 10 start lines clean, no face-flip. The signal was at ARRIVAL: 2 misses and 2 lip-hangs, all four on dying pace, both misses on the pull side. Read at the time as soft-pace drift rather than a stroke fault. This is the ONLY scored putting benchmark in the entire project, and it is on a putter that went back — so the 20-ball five-footer in the Short Putts plan has no prior number to beat, only this one for context, and it was hit from four feet rather than five with a different head in hand. Treat it as a marker, not a baseline.

THE REST, in one line each. JUL 17, ground-level close-up, 3 strokes: tempo ~1:1, face closing, early lift, contact centred. JUL 18, face-on / near-DTL, 2 strokes: path near-neutral, start line on centre, early lift PRONOUNCED. JUL 18 baseline re-analysis of all 10 original clips (Phantom 7.5, three angles): early lift documented from all three — steep rise going back, head hanging high after impact, exiting the frame upward in the side view; old backswing ≈0.40s against ≈0.65s later the same week, a ~60% longer load; path straight and on-line in every old overhead, so the stroke's bones were always good; face-closing too subtle to confirm at that frame rate. JUL 18, DF3i first filmed reps, 5 eye-level overhead clips: start line dead centre 5 of 5, no left pull anywhere, tempo 0.55s back / 0.23s down ≈ 2.4:1. JUL 21, DF3i, 5 ground-level DTL clips through a tunnel-and-gate drill: start line on the centre line 5 of 5, gated centre every time with no left leak, face square through impact, and the first ground-level look at head height — the head stayed low and extended down the line, none of the abrupt lift-and-hang from the baseline clips.

WHAT THIS CHANGES ABOUT LIVE FINDINGS: nothing. Path SETTLED, tempo FIXED at 2.0:1, early lift CLOSED — all three were re-measured on the LINK on Jul 30, which is a session that survives. The pre-LINK film was the road to those answers, not the answers themselves.

ONE THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE EVOLUTION GRID. Its five columns — S1, S2, S3, S4, BL — ARE these deleted sessions, so the Putting Lab's stroke-evolution table is now entirely pre-LINK and stops before the putter you play. It still reads correctly as history. Rebuilding it on the Jul 30 and Aug 10 LINK sessions is a separate decision and has not been made.

ALSO KEPT ON PURPOSE, and worth saying since they involve retired putters: the AUG 1 Beekman entry (DF3i, ON COURSE, no film — it is the 'pace felt dialled' report that un-benched a putter returned nine days later, and this project keeps that as a standing counter-example to trusting feel), and the AUG 10 session, which is a DF3i-vs-LINK A/B and therefore the comparison that decided the putter, as well as the source of the current start-line numbers.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — Why reading got a plan when nothing measures it
sections.k: The routine's first step handed off to nothing, and reading is the front half of the pace problem — two structural reasons, and no measured one.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. The putting lab already had five plans in a clean situation split. Was green reading a real gap or just a missing chapter?

WHAT ARGUED AGAINST IT. Nothing in the record measures Jack's reading. No fault, no film, no logged mis-read. By the standard this project usually applies, that is thin ground for a page — and a plan built to complete a set is exactly the kind of padding the round-prep rules warn about.

WHAT DECIDED IT, and neither reason is 'greens get read'. First, the Routine plan opens with READ IT FROM BEHIND and then handed off to nothing at all — the first step of his own routine was the only one without a page behind it, while grip, the short stroke and the long stroke had all been split out. Second, SPEED PICKS THE LINE: a putt has a different line at every pace, so the read cannot be settled before the pace is chosen. That makes reading the front half of the pace problem, and pace is the one open putting fault on the card.

HOW IT IS WRITTEN AS A RESULT. Labelled general best practice on every section, with the one exception called out — 'inside six feet, stop reading once you have the fall line' exists because of his documented short-putt history, not because it is standard advice. It deliberately sets NO pace of its own; the two stroke plans own that, and a third source for pace is how a retired cue survives.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT HIS. Logging which SIDE missed putts finish on. Clustering low means the read is under-done. Clustering left inside six feet is aim, and that belongs to the laser audit rather than to this page.

NOT MEASURED: everything on that plan, plus the 8–9 stimp its speed talk is calibrated against, which remains an estimate. Full cross-lab reasoning — including the four plans that were rejected — is in the SWING workshop log, since the review covered both labs at once.

sections.t: Aug 14 2026 — The laser: what it can measure, and the trap that came in the box
sections.k: It can finally put a number on ‘barely open’ — but only as a measuring device, only after it is calibrated to the face, and only if you never look at the beam.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. Jack bought a PUTTLAZR green-line indoor putting trainer (Aug 13). What can it actually settle, and what should it be kept away from?

WHAT IT IS.
