sections.t: THE CLAW IS OUT — what you play now
sections.k: Conventional on every length again, your call — and the short-putt change is a choke-down, which is a smaller lever rather than a different hold.
sections.b:
FROM YOU, Sep 12 2026, and authoritative: the claw is out, you hated it, and what you are doing on the short ones instead is choking up a little on the handle. That is a decision about what you DO, so it is the instruction on this card from today, it is not on trial, and it is not waiting on a scoreboard.

WHAT YOU PLAY NOW. CONVENTIONAL (reverse overlap) on every length — the hold you have had all year, described in full in GRIP & POSTURE — and inside about six feet you grip DOWN the handle a little. Nothing else on this card moved: the pop stroke is still the open question, 17 inches past is still the speed, and barely open still does the aiming.

THE CLAW LASTED TWO DAYS AND COST THE RECORD NOTHING, which is the one genuinely clean thing about this and is worth saying plainly. No claw rep was ever filmed or scored on this putter — the 20-ball five-footer was owed on Sep 10 and it is still owed now — so there is no orphaned block of numbers, no baseline to unwind, and nothing anywhere in the app that was measured on it. Two days cost an instruction, not data.

AND THE OLD BASELINE IS NOT GONE AFTER ALL. The Sep 10 version of this card retired every conventional short-putt number in the project on the grounds that they belonged to a different grip. They belong to THIS grip again, so the reason for setting them aside has evaporated. They are still thin, and the best of them — 8 out of 10 from four feet, Jul 20, still the only scored putting benchmark anywhere in the record — was made on the DF3i, which is a different putter. Thin and old is not the same as void.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and it is TWO things rather than the one the last version of this card claimed. The POP STROKE, unchanged, and still the reason this plan has a scoreboard at all. And HOW FAR DOWN you grip, which is new, which nobody has put a number on, and which changes the pace — see CHOKING DOWN below. 'A little' is exactly the kind of word this project has watched drift before: 'barely open' has been on the aim card since Aug 10 and still has no number on it either.

sections.t: SIX FEET — where the line actually falls
sections.k: Six is the line this plan already drew and the app already counts to, so the boundary needs no new judgment — and where there is doubt it falls to conventional.
sections.b:
Your words were "maybe 6ft and less", and the hedge is fair: nobody paces a putt off before deciding how to hold the club. What makes six workable is that it is not a new number. This plan has been quarantined inside about six feet since Aug 13, the Lag Putts plan starts past it, and the app's own putting buckets break in exactly the same place — inside three feet, then four to six, then seven to twelve. So the choke-down's range is the two shortest buckets, and every putt you log already records which side of the line it was on. Nothing has to be added to the logger for this decision to become checkable.

THE DECISION RULE ON THE GREEN, because "about six feet" is a judgment and you make it standing over the ball with no tape measure. IF YOU ARE UNSURE, IT IS A LAG — go conventional. The asymmetry is real and it runs one way. The cost of a choked handle on a putt that turns out to be long is a SHORTER LEVER on the exact shot where pace is your open fault — less club to move the ball, on the one putt where distance is the whole problem. The cost of a full-length handle on a putt that turns out to be short is that you held it exactly where you have held it all year. One of those two mistakes lands on the thing you are trying to measure; the other does not. Let the doubt fall toward conventional.

WHAT WOULD MOVE THE LINE. Only the scoreboard. If choked blocks come back better at eight and ten feet as well, then six is the wrong number and it moves — but it moves on MAKES, not on how it feels out there, because a choke that feels good at ten feet is precisely how a lever gets shortened on a pace putt without anybody noticing it happened.

sections.t: WHAT THE POP STROKE ACTUALLY IS
sections.k: A short backstroke and a firm rap with little follow-through — and it was invented for slow greens, which is what you play.
sections.b:
The pop stroke is a short backstroke, a firm accelerating rap at the ball, and an abbreviated follow-through. Gary Player played it, rapping the ball with almost no finish. Billy Casper is the purest example — compact, hands close to the body, the face hooded going back, and then a pop; the standard description is that it looks like tapping a tack with a hammer, which is why it is also called the tap stroke.

The part worth knowing before you adopt it: this stroke came out of SLOW GREENS. It was developed by players who needed extra pop to get the ball to the hole on surfaces that did not run. That is a genuine argument in its favour for you — your pace is calibrated at an estimated 8-9 stimp, which is exactly that world. It is also the warning that comes with it. On a fast green a stroke built to add force is the wrong instinct, and you will find that out on a downhill four-footer before you find it out anywhere else.

Your own description of it — short back, SHORT through — is the same shape Casper played, minus the mechanism that made it work for him. It describes the SIZE of the stroke and nothing about the hands, which is exactly the half worth borrowing.

sections.t: THE ONE THING YOU CANNOT COPY — the wrists
sections.k: Casper's pop was a wrist stroke; on this putter it has to be a short shoulder stroke instead, or it fights everything else you do.
sections.b:
This is the whole adaptation, and it is not a small one. The classic pop stroke is a WRIST stroke. Casper cocked his wrists to keep the face square going back and then released them into the ball. The technique's own history says as much: it was right-wrist action that supplied the extra pop on slow greens.

That mechanism is not available to you, for two reasons that point the same way. Your whole method is QUIET HANDS with the shoulders running the stroke. And the head you play is built on the premise that the face squares ITSELF when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own instruction is that your job is only to let it stay square. A wrist-released pop is the single most hand-active stroke in putting. Bolting it onto a zero-torque putter is asking the club to undo what you are doing to it.

So take the GEOMETRY, not the MECHANISM. Short backstroke, short through-stroke — your call, and it is the authentic shape; Casper's finish stopped dead. Both halves run from the shoulders, with the wrists silent — exactly the stroke you already make, just shorter and more committed. What you are borrowing from Casper is the SIZE and the INTENT, and nothing else.

The tell that you have drifted into the real thing is the putter head PASSING YOUR HANDS. That is the wrist releasing, and it is the one thing to watch for. FOR TWO DAYS IT WAS GUARDED BY GEOMETRY — a trail hand that is off the handle cannot flip the one it is not holding — and as of Sep 12 it is guarded by DISCIPLINE again, because your trail hand is back on the club. That is a real loss and it belongs here rather than in the small print: taking the trail hand out was the claw's one mechanical advantage, and choking down does not replace it. It shortens the lever; it does not remove a hand. So watch the head against your hands on the short ones the way you did before Sep 10.

sections.t: SHORT THROUGH IS NOT THE SAME AS QUITTING
sections.k: A short finish that accelerated and a short finish that decelerated look identical afterwards — the ball's roll-out is what tells them apart.
sections.b:
This is the one thing to get right about a short finish, because the good version and the bad version leave the same picture.

THE GOOD ONE: the head accelerates through the ball and then stops, because the stroke was small and the energy went into the ball. That is Casper's stroke, and it is what you have asked for.

THE BAD ONE: the head slows down BEFORE the ball and the finish is short because there was nothing left. That is deceleration — the classic short-putt killer, and the thing a short backstroke makes easy to fall into, since a small backstroke gives you less room to build any speed at all.

Afterwards they look the same. So do not judge it by the finish. JUDGE IT BY THE ROLL-OUT: a stroke that accelerated gets the ball consistently to 17 inches past. A stroke that quit leaves putts short and, worse, leaves them short by a varying amount. If your short putts start finishing at the front edge, the through-stroke is quitting, and the fix is committing to the pace rather than lengthening the backstroke.

The useful mental version: the backstroke sets the size, the through-stroke sets the INTENT. Short is a size. Quitting is a loss of intent, and it is a different thing entirely.

sections.t: SPEED — 17 inches past, and why firm is right on the short ones
sections.k: The ring around the hole is trodden flat, so a dying ball wobbles through it — 17 inches past is the researched target.
sections.b:
There is a real reason a firmer short putt works, and it is not toughness. The area roughly one to six feet all around a hole takes all the foot traffic on a green, so it is depressed and bumpy — Dave Pelz's 'lumpy donut'. A ball arriving with barely any pace wobbles through exactly the bit of green that is in the worst condition. A ball with a little more speed pushes through it.

Pelz's number is 17 INCHES PAST the hole. That is the target: enough pace to hold the line through the trodden ring and take some break out, not so much that you shrink the effective hole and leave yourself the one coming back.

The honest counter-argument, because it is real physics: a ball dying into the hole can fall in off the edges, so a softer putt has a bigger effective target and more room for a stroke error. Both things are true. The reason firm wins on a SHORT putt specifically is that inside six feet you are not solving a distance problem — you are trying to start it on line and get it there before the green can do anything to it. That balance flips as soon as the putt gets long, which is why this stroke is quarantined.

17 inches is a specific number, so treat it as one: on the practice green, put a tee 17 inches behind the hole and putt to leave it between the hole and the tee.

sections.t: THE LOFT TRAP — when the rap becomes a jab
sections.k: A firm short stroke is the easiest way to lean the shaft forward, and this face has 2° to give before the ball is being driven into the turf.
sections.b:
This is the specific way the pop stroke can hurt you on THIS putter, and it is worth more attention than the stroke shape.

Casper's pop hit the ball and then the turf, clubhead stopping abruptly. That is a descending, forward-leaning delivery. Your putter is built around 0° shaft lean, so a rap arriving with the shaft leaning forward delofts a face that has little to lose — and a delofted putt is driven into the turf: it skids, then rolls, and finishes short and off line.

Its loft is 2°, CONFIRMED — L.A.B. publishes 2° effective loft for this head in the SPECIFICATIONS panel of the LINK.2.1 custom build page — confirmed Aug 14, so this is a spec now, not an inference. The arithmetic is no longer directional: you have 2° to spend and a forward-leaning delivery spends it fast. This section was written when the figure was an inference; the number came back the same, which is why nothing it told you to do has changed.

The rule does not relax because the stroke got shorter. SHAFT VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT — the same on this stroke as on every other one.

AND AS OF SEP 12 THERE IS ONE SUSPECT ON THIS CARD AGAIN. Between Aug 25 and Sep 10 there was one: the forward press had come out — the trigger is a re-grip, which moves pressure rather than the shaft — leaving the pop as the only move that could lean this face forward. The claw was briefly a second, because a claw can creep the handle forward without you feeling it. It is out, so the pop is the only suspect again and the diagnostic cleanliness this card lost on Sep 10 comes straight back. The scuff is still worth listening for here more than anywhere on the green, because the pop still lives on this card and nowhere else.

CHOKING DOWN IS NOT A THIRD SUSPECT, and the reason is worth knowing rather than assuming. Gripping lower moves your hands DOWN the shaft; it does not by itself tilt the shaft FORWARD, and forward lean is what delofts the face. What a choke can change instead is the LIE — hands lower with the same bend sits the toe up — and that is a different failure with a different check: the BLADE, not the shaft. It has its own line in the rules and its own check in GRIP & POSTURE under 'The blade tells you'.

The check needs no camera: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click. A driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you start hearing the scuff on short putts, the pop has turned into a jab and the shaft is leaning. The camera version is the same face-on clip you already owe — shaft angle at address against shaft angle at impact, same number both times.

sections.t: CHOKING DOWN — what you now play
sections.k: Standard practice for short putts and a sound answer to a hand you want quieter — but the amount has no number on it, and the thing it changes most is pace.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, CHECKED AGAINST STANDARD PRACTICE.

WHAT YOU SAID, Sep 12 2026: the claw is out, you hated it, and you are just kind of choking up a little on the short ones. Your intent is the instruction and nothing below overrides it — what follows is what the textbook says about the same move, so you can see where you are on it and where you are on your own.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS. Gripping down the handle on short putts is ordinary, taught and common on tour. It does three things, and only the first is the one people usually mean. It SHORTENS THE LEVER, so the same hand movement produces a smaller swing and less ball speed — more control, less power, which is the right way round inside six feet where there is no distance problem to solve. It brings your hands CLOSER TO THE BALL, which most players read as more connected and more precise. And it makes the club feel LIGHTER in the head, because you have taken shaft out from under your hands, which quietens a hand that wants to hit at it. On a putt that only has to reach the hole on line, every one of those is pointed the right way.

SO THE VERDICT IS THAT YOU ARE ON TRACK, and that is a real verdict rather than a polite one: this is the standard move for the exact problem, it asks nothing of you that the rest of the card fights, and unlike the claw it changes no hold you have spent a year learning. It is also a much smaller change than the claw was, which is worth noticing given what the claw was supposed to buy.

WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and this is where it differs from the grip it replaced. THE TRAIL HAND IS BACK ON THE CLUB. The claw's whole argument was mechanical: with the trail hand off the handle, flipping the face is awkward rather than merely discouraged, which suits a head built on the premise that the face squares itself once the hands stop interfering. Choking down buys none of that. Quiet hands is a discipline again, not a geometry. If the flick comes back, this is why.

THE COST, and it lands on the open fault. A shorter lever means the SAME STROKE LENGTH SENDS THE BALL LESS FAR. Your whole distance system is stroke length at a fixed tempo, so choking down moves the calibration on every putt you play choked — including the 17 inches past that this card sets as the speed. That number was learned at full length. Re-learn it choked, or it will read as a putt coming up short and you will blame the through-stroke.

PUT A NUMBER ON 'A LITTLE'. This is the one thing to actually do, and it costs a minute: MARK THE HANDLE where your lead hand sits, or measure it once in inches and write it down. An unmeasured amount is an amount that drifts, and a choke that drifts is a pace variable hiding inside a line fix — which, with pace as the standing open fault, is the one kind of drift this project can least afford. 'Barely open' has been on the aim card since Aug 10 without a number and is still unconfirmed; do not start a second one.

AND CHECK THE BLADE ONCE. Hands lower with the same bend can sit the toe up, and this head is built to balance to its lie. Set up choked, look at the sole, and if the toe is off the ground get a touch lower or stand a touch closer until it sits flat. One look settles it — it is the check GRIP & POSTURE already carries under 'The blade tells you', pointed at a new cause.

sections.t: WHY THIS STAYS INSIDE SIX FEET
sections.k: The pop holds the backstroke short and varies force, which is the exact failure the lag plan exists to prevent.
sections.b:
Your distance system says DISTANCE COMES FROM STROKE LENGTH AT A FIXED TEMPO. The Lag Putts plan names the opposite as the failure mode by name: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else.

A pop stroke is that failure mode, deliberately. It holds the length short and supplies the rest with force.

On a short putt that is not a flaw, because there is no meaningful distance problem to solve inside six feet — the ball has one job, which is to reach the hole on line. On anything longer it is exactly the thing that produced a round of short lags and hot short putts, and it is why pace has never been calibrated in this project.

So the split is hard: inside about six feet is this plan, outside it is the Lag Putts plan. Keeping them apart is what keeps the ladder numbers clean — the ladder is measuring the long stroke, and a pop rep on it is a corrupted data point.

WHAT CHANGES AT THAT LINE, AS OF SEP 12. The HOLD is the same on both sides again — conventional everywhere — so the two-grips problem the Sep 10 version created has gone. What still differs at six feet is the stroke shape and now a choke on the handle, which is a smaller difference than a grip change and is not nothing: a choked five-footer and a full-length thirty-footer are still not the same club length. So read the two sets side by side with that in mind rather than treating them as one series. Each side of the line is still measured against itself, which is how both were always going to be used.

sections.t: WHAT IT FIXES, AND WHAT IT DOESN'T
sections.k: Between them they cure deceleration, the freeze and the trail hand — neither of them cures your aim.
sections.b:
WHAT IT GENUINELY HELPS. Deceleration, which is the classic short-putt killer, and the freeze — a short committed stroke gives the conscious mind less time and less room to intervene. That connects to the trigger work: your failure lives on short putts under pressure, not on the practice green, and a stroke with less dwell and less distance to travel is a real answer to that.

WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH, and this matters because it would be easy to expect otherwise. Your left miss is an AIM error, not a delivery error — reclassified Aug 10, and the Aug 10 pm mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right with no bias at all. Face angle decides about 80% of where a putt starts. A pop stroke changes how the face is DELIVERED; it does not change where you have AIMED it. Barely open is still what does the aiming, and it is untouched by any of this.

So do not expect the left ones to stop — and that goes for the choke-down exactly as much as for the pop. Moving your hands down the handle moves where the hands ARE; it does not move where you have AIMED. The choke is worth playing because a shorter lever suits a putt that only has to reach the hole on line, and the pop is worth testing because a short committed stroke under pressure is worth having. Neither is worth anything as an answer to the left miss, which is barely open's job and is untouched by any of this.

sections.t: THE SCOREBOARD — the 20-ball five-footer
sections.k: Two blocks in the same session, both choked down, differing only in the stroke — and the conventional numbers already on file are a comparison again rather than history.
sections.b:
This does not get decided on feel. The whole project's record on deciding putting things by feel is four putter movements in twelve days.

THE TEST. 20 balls from five feet, in two blocks in the SAME session: one block with the pop stroke, one with your normal stroke length. SAME GRIP AND SAME CHOKE ON BOTH — conventional, gripped down to your mark — so the stroke is the only thing that differs. Same green, same day: green speed changes everything and a comparison across two sessions compares two greens.

RUN THE NORMAL-STROKE BLOCK FIRST. It is one arm of the pop-stroke test, and it is also the first number this putter has from five feet with anything written down about how you were holding it.

WHAT TO LOG. Makes out of 20, the direction of every miss, the green speed — and the CHOKE you used, because a block run at an unrecorded grip height cannot be repeated. The left-miss pass mark the grip experiment set — 2 or fewer LEFT misses per 20 — reads across, because it is a test of aim and aim has not changed. The MAKE count reads across with a caveat rather than not at all: the conventional figures on file are the same hold you are playing now, but the best of them was made on the DF3i, so the putter differs even though the grip no longer does.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CONVICT IT. More makes is the headline, but watch three other things. If the misses get LONGER — running well past — the pop is a jab and the loft trap has you. If putts come up SHORT, the through-stroke is quitting rather than merely being short, which is the failure mode a short finish invites. And if you start hearing the scuff, stop and check the shaft before you read the scores at all.

Run it at two green speeds before you commit. A stroke built for slow greens will flatter itself on a slow one.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: Where the stroke came from, what was adapted, and what has not been measured.
sections.b:
SEP 12 2026, FROM YOU AND AUTHORITATIVE: the claw is out — you hated it — and you are choking up a little on the short ones instead. Conventional on every length again. What that undid, in this plan: the two-blocks-both-claw test is now two blocks both CHOKED; the wrist guard goes from geometry back to discipline, which is a real loss and the claw's only mechanical advantage; the LOFT TRAP drops from two suspects back to one, since a choke moves the hands down the shaft rather than leaning it; and the conventional short-putt numbers the Sep 10 card retired are live again, because they are this grip. What it added: a second open dial — HOW FAR DOWN — with no number on it, and a pace consequence, because a shorter lever sends the same stroke length less far and the 17 inches was learned at full length. Your report from the day: 32 putts, and you called it good. That is one round, it is your own card rather than a test, and it cannot separate the choke from everything else about the day — the same shape as 'pace felt dialled' on Aug 1, which un-benched a putter that went back nine days later. It is not why the claw is out; you are.

SEP 10 2026 — THE CLAW, FOR TWO DAYS. 'Claw grip from now on for short putts. Maybe 6ft and less.' It was adopted by decision rather than by measurement, and it was reversed the same way before any measurement existed: no claw rep was ever filmed or scored on this putter, so nothing in the record was built on it and nothing had to be unwound. The four-block test order had collapsed to two blocks both claw; the reserve-grip framing was retired across GRIP & POSTURE, the ROUTINE plan and LAG PUTTS; the ladder and short-putt numbers were declared non-comparable. All of it is reversed above. The cost of the episode was two days of instruction and a handful of plan rewrites — worth recording because the same trade will come up again.

Aug 25: the forward press came out by your decision (a re-grip trigger instead), so this plan's shaft rule goes back to ADDRESS AND IMPACT alongside the ROUTINE and GRIP & POSTURE plans, and the press-plus-pop pairing that the LOFT TRAP called the highest-risk on the card is down to the pop alone. The risk did not fall — the number of things that could be causing it did.

Aug 14, later: the 2° loft this plan's LOFT TRAP section is built on was confirmed from L.A.B.'s specifications, having been an inference since Jul 30. The estimate was right, so no instruction moved — the section now states it as a spec.

Aug 14: the forward press came back as the trigger, so this plan's shaft rule was re-scoped from 'address and impact' to IMPACT, matching the ROUTINE and GRIP & POSTURE plans. The pop-plus-press combination is now called out in the LOFT TRAP section as the highest-risk pairing on the card.

FROM YOU, Aug 13 2026, and authoritative: a pop stroke on the short ones — short back, SHORT through, and no wrists. Also from you, same day: the claw is out of play as the running grip. CORRECTED shortly after to 'another short-putt SOLUTION you are trying, not a safety net' — and SUPERSEDED on Sep 10, when it became the grip. Both of those framings are history now; the top of this file carries what stands. The plan was retitled off the pop stroke because of it: two candidates are on trial, and naming the plan after one of them made the other look like a contingency.

RESEARCHED. The pop stroke's history and mechanics: Gary Player rapped it with no follow-through; Billy Casper is the canonical version — compact, hands close to the body, face hooded going back, ball-then-turf contact and an abbreviated finish, described as tapping a tack with a hammer. Its origin is slow greens, where right-wrist action supplied the extra pop. The speed target comes from Dave Pelz's research: the 'lumpy donut' of trodden ground one to six feet around the hole, and 17 inches past as the optimal pace. The counter-argument — that a dying ball has a bigger effective hole — is real physics and is stated rather than buried.

ADAPTED, and this is the significant edit. The classic pop is a WRIST stroke, which contradicts both quiet hands and the zero-torque premise of the LINK. What survives here is the geometry — short backstroke, positive through-stroke — run from the shoulders. That is a reasoned adaptation, not something anyone measured.

REVISED SAME DAY. An earlier version of this plan had the through-stroke 'at least as long as the backstroke' and the claw running as the guardrail. Both were corrected by you: the finish is short, and the grip is conventional. The anti-deceleration guard therefore moved from LENGTH to ACCELERATION, which is the honest version anyway. The wrist-flick guard went to discipline with the claw out, came back to geometry with it on Sep 10, and went back to discipline on Sep 12 when the claw did.

NOT MEASURED. All of it. No pop-stroke rep has ever been filmed or scored on this putter, the 20-ball five-footer has not been run on the LINK at all, and the face-on clip that would catch the shaft leaning forward is still owed — ONE clip again as of Sep 12, since there is one grip to shoot rather than two. The claw joined this list on Sep 10 and left it on Sep 12 without ever producing a number, which is the whole story of it. The choke-down joins it today: unmeasured, and additionally unRECORDED until you mark the handle. Until the scoreboard exists this plan describes an experiment, not a finding.

ADDED with that reframe, RETIRED on Sep 10: the two-dials section at the top and its four-combination test order (baseline, pop only, claw only, both). The reasoning behind it never retired and it applies to the new pair: changing two things at once is the error that ran through the entire putter saga. The two dials today are the STROKE and the CHOKE HEIGHT, so the scoreboard still runs as two blocks — and the choke has to be the SAME on both of them, which is the second reason to mark the handle. An unmarked choke turns a one-variable test back into a two-variable one without anybody deciding to.

briefing.focus: Everything that is true before the putter moves, in one place: how you stand, what is in your hands, where the ball is, and where the low point ends up. The GRIP is CONVENTIONAL on every length again as of Sep 12 — the claw is out, your call — with the handle gripped DOWN a little inside about six feet, which changes where your hands sit rather than how they hold it, so everything on this card is true on every putt. One mechanism runs through the rest of it — lead-side pressure pins the low point, the low point decides whether the ball rolls or hops, and ball position plus a vertical shaft decide where that low point meets the ball. Keep any feel that passes the four checks. The routine that sits on top of this is the Putting Routine plan.
rules: GET LOW — the deep bend is what presents the lie this putter needs
CONVENTIONAL on every length (Sep 12 — the claw is out) — grip DOWN the handle inside ~6 ft
Ball 1–2 BALL-WIDTHS inside the lead heel — mark it
HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — that IS the straight shaft
NO FORWARD PRESS (Aug 25) — the trigger is a RE-GRIP, so the shaft is VERTICAL at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
QUIET HANDS — the shoulders run the stroke, the hands just hold on
Pressure ~55/45 LEAD — its one job is pinning the low point
TRAIL FOOT back — square will feel closed
TRAIL HAND senses the weight on LAGS ONLY — it never pushes, and nothing releases

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.k: Bend over and get low — the anchor feel everything else hangs off, and it is what switches the putter's technology on.
sections.b:
Your words, and they go at the top: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

Two mechanisms under the feel. FIRST — the LINK is Lie Angle Balanced, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at its built lie (69° lie, ~2° effective loft — an estimate, see the Notes — 0° lean, 34"). Stand tall or reach and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its lie, and the self-squaring property you bought quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology.

SECOND — more bend hangs the arms freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall builds in an arc you don't want.

sections.t: THE GRIP — what is actually in your hands
sections.k: Conventional on every length, light pressure, and a choke down the handle on the short ones — and the light pressure is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference.
sections.b:
ONE GRIP, EVERY LENGTH. As of Sep 12 the claw is OUT — your call, you hated it — and conventional (reverse overlap) is the hold on every putt again. What changes inside about six feet is not the hold but WHERE ON THE HANDLE it sits: you grip down a little. That is a lever change, not a grip change, so every word on this card applies to it unaltered. The choke's own detail lives in the SHORT PUTTS plan, because that is the only place it is used.

IF YOU ARE UNSURE WHICH SIDE OF SIX FEET YOU ARE ON, IT IS A LAG — full length on the handle. The reasoning is in the Short Putts plan; the short version is that a choke shortens the lever, and a shorter lever on a putt that turns out to be long lands on pace, which is the open fault.

LIGHT PRESSURE, and this is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a preference. A Lie Angle Balanced head is built so the face squares itself when the hands stop interfering — L.A.B.'s own coaching is that your job is only to let it stay square, and their first drill is putting with your thumbs off the grip. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one.

THE ZERO-LEAN GRIP GEOMETRY. This putter carries a LAMKIN DEEP ETCHED — zero built-in lean. The shaft stands vertical and your hands sit about 1.35" behind the ball's centre, and that is correct rather than something to fix. The DF3i's 'hands EVEN with the ball' cue belonged to its Press Pistol 2°, which leaned the shaft for you; that grip went back with that putter and the cue died with it. Never carry it across.

THE TRAIL HAND — YOURS, CHECKED. You proposed this one: on LAGS, conventional grip, with the RIGHT hand sensing the weight of the head and the left just riding along. Keep it — it is a good cue and it is pointed at the right fault. It is not standard putting instruction, but it survived a check against L.A.B.'s own quiet-hands design, and the instruction you paired it with — 'let the head release' — was cut precisely because that half contradicts a zero-torque head. Pace is the open one, distance on this putter is stroke LENGTH at a fixed tempo, and a hand that reports how heavy the head feels going back is reporting the exact thing the ladder exists to calibrate.

SENSE the weight, never PUSH the club. A trail hand that drives through the ball is a second pace input stacked on stroke length, and it has a quiet way of shoving the handle forward — which breaks the vertical-shaft rule without ever feeling like it did. THIS IS A LAG CUE, and it stays one now the trail hand is back on the club inside six feet. Between Sep 10 and Sep 12 it was kept out of the short ones because a claw has no feel hand at all; that reason has gone and the original one has not. Inside six feet there is no distance to feel, so there is nothing for the cue to do and it can only add a pace input to a putt that needs none.

AND THE OWED CLIP IS ONE CLIP AGAIN. Between Sep 10 and Sep 12 the face-on clip had to be shot on both grips, because a claw creeps the handle forward without announcing it. One grip, one answer: address against impact, and the only thing left that can lean this shaft is the pop stroke on the short ones.

sections.t: THE SETUP — the four checks
sections.k: Ball inside the lead heel · low point just behind it · shaft back to vertical · 55/45. Pass all four and keep your feel.
sections.b:
BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. BALL one to two ball-widths inside the lead heel — forward of centre so the head is a hair ASCENDING at contact, which is what produces true roll. Mark the spot and keep it; launch is sensitive to it, and a ball position that wanders reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine. Weight stacked ON the ball. TRAIL FOOT a touch back. Rock the shoulders, QUIET HANDS, loose grip. Face set BARELY OPEN — its own section below.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER — shaft straight up and down. That is the entire hands instruction. Don't add lean to make it look like a normal putter: this face carries little loft and is delivered at 0° lean, so there is nothing to spare, and a driven ball skids before it rolls and finishes short.

(A vertical shaft photographs as hands ~1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball from face to centre plus the riser hosel's offset. Same position, the camera's description of it. Ball position is set by your FEET; the shaft is set by your HANDS.)

(1) BALL one to two ball-widths INSIDE THE LEAD HEEL. Use the heel, not a body reference — a deep-bend posture moves your chest line; the heel doesn't move. Mark it on the mat.

(2) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the head is a HAIR ascending at contact. This is what ball position is for.

(3) SHAFT RETURNS TO VERTICAL at impact — the same place it started.

(4) PRESSURE about 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much you start steering.

If a feel you're comfortable in delivers all four, keep the feel. The checks are the rule; the feel is yours.

sections.t: WEIGHT AND THE LOW POINT — the mechanism under all of it
sections.k: Lead pressure pins where the stroke bottoms out, and hanging back adds loft you never asked for.
sections.b:
Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the putter meets the ball. Everything below follows from that, on any head.

Weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so the head arrives climbing hard with the shaft leaning away from the target. That adds loft you never asked for: the ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then rolls. Every bit of hop is energy that was supposed to become roll, so the putt arrives soft — and skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your pace stops being repeatable between surfaces.

The window on this head is narrow in both directions, because a putter's loft budget is small to start with. Lean away from the target and you add loft; lean toward it and you go below zero and drive the ball down. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a skidding ball that finishes short of what the stroke intended.

sections.t: THE SHAFT — vertical at address and at impact
sections.k: Nothing moves you off vertical any more, so address is a real check again — and both ends have to read the same number.
sections.b:
The shaft is VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND VERTICAL AT IMPACT. Impact is the end that matters, and address is a fair proxy for it again as of Aug 25: the forward press is out and the trigger is a RE-GRIP (it lives in the ROUTINE plan), which changes what is in your hands rather than where the shaft is. Nothing takes you off vertical on purpose any more, so nothing has to be given back — and the two ends reading the same number is the whole test. Forward at IMPACT delofts a face with little to give and drives the ball into the turf — it skids, then rolls, and finishes short. Hands falling BACK invite the wrist flick. Both directions off vertical at impact are misses.

Check with a camera: one face-on clip, shaft angle at address versus impact, same number both times — pass. ONE GRIP, ONE CLIP as of Sep 12: the two-grip version of this check went out with the claw. Check without a camera: LISTEN. A purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a driven ball adds a faint scuff a beat later. If you hear the scuff, the shaft leaned forward, whatever your hands report.

Two different variables, two different controls. Ball position is set by your FEET (check 1). Shaft lean at impact is set by your HANDS (check 3), and the target is zero.

A vertical shaft photographs as the hands sitting about 1.35" behind the ball's centre — half a ball (0.84") from face to centre, plus roughly half an inch from shaft axis to face on this riser-hosel blade. That's not a position to set; it's what 'hands over the head of the putter' produces on its own. If you try to put the hands somewhere, you're adding lean. Nothing in the routine asks you to any more, which is the point of a trigger that lives in your grip pressure instead.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — set it back
sections.k: Trail foot back, square will feel closed — and always face first, then stance.
sections.b:
Set the trail foot a touch further back than feels natural, and expect square to feel CLOSED. You're recalibrating off an open baseline, so trust the line you set rather than the feel for the first few sessions.

Why it matters this much: in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. An open stance doesn't just aim you left — it points the whole stroke left, and then either the hands steer the takeaway to save it, or the ball starts left. A stance error shows up disguised as a takeaway problem.

Ten-second check: alignment stick down the line, toes PARALLEL, not converging. And keep the order religiously — aim the FACE to the spot first, then build the stance around it. Face-first means a creeping stance shows up as discomfort, and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: The blade tells you
sections.k: This head reports a bad strike instead of muffling it — use that, then measure.
sections.b:
A narrow blade carries less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds real distance and you can FEEL it. That makes your hands a better instrument on this putter than on a big mallet — a mediocre low point won't hide.

Use it, but don't stop there. The sound check costs nothing: one clean click is a rolling ball; a faint scuff a beat later is a driven one. The measurement is the tape test — twelve minutes, its own plan — and it's the thing to run before drawing any conclusion about this putter's pace.

AND IT ANSWERS THE ONE QUESTION THE CHOKE-DOWN RAISES. Gripping lower with the same bend can sit the toe up, and this head is built to balance to its lie — so the first time you set up choked, look at the sole. Flat is the pass. Toe off the ground means get a touch lower or stand a touch closer until it sits down. It is one look, once, not a thing to check every putt.

sections.t: Settle any change with data
sections.k: A/B it on the ladder and let the stopping points decide, not the feel.
sections.b:
A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: current feel. Block B: the change, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread; tighter spread wins, and that's the answer, not anyone's opinion.

FACE-ON CLIP — the one measurement this plan keeps asking for, and since Sep 10 it is TWO clips, one per grip: shaft angle at address versus impact (matching at address and impact is the pass, and as of Aug 25 that is the plain question again — nothing in the routine moves the shaft, and the grip has no built-in lean either, so whatever the tape shows IS your hands), where the head bottoms out relative to the ball, and ball position rep to rep. White tape on the shaft, 240 fps, camera at ball height square to the line.

sections.t: Notes — the paper trail
sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes the checks above.
sections.b:
SEP 12 2026 — the claw is OUT after two days, your call, and conventional is the grip on every length again. This card goes back to one grip: the six-foot split it grew on Sep 10 is gone, and what happens at six feet now is a CHOKE, which is where the hands sit rather than how they hold. The owed face-on clip drops back to one grip. The trail-hand feel cue stays a LAG cue — the claw was briefly a second reason for that and the original reason still stands on its own. Everything else on this card never moved through either change: the bend, the ball position, the vertical shaft, the trail foot, the pressure, the low point. A new line joined 'The blade tells you': check the sole sits flat once you grip down.

SEP 10 2026 — the claw came back as the running grip inside about six feet for two days, which split this card's grip rule at six feet and doubled the owed clip. Reversed Sep 12, above. No claw rep was ever filmed or scored, so nothing on this card was ever measured on it.

Aug 25: the forward press is out by your decision — a late release and re-grip instead — so this plan's shaft rule reverts to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, which is where it stood before Aug 14. The reasoning that re-scoped it to impact alone is not wrong and is not retired; it simply has nothing to act on while nothing moves the hands off vertical. New guard, and it belongs to this plan because this is where grip pressure lives: re-grip to the SAME LIGHT PRESSURE you released, because a firmer regrab is a trail hand back in the stroke.

Aug 14: the forward press returned by your decision, so this plan's 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule is retired and the shaft rule re-scoped to IMPACT. What did NOT change: the mechanism. A shaft still leaning at impact still delofts and still finishes short — the press is only safe because it recovers, and that recovery is UNFILMED. The face-on address-versus-impact clip is now the owed measurement rather than a nice-to-have.

The 'hands level or a touch ahead at impact' rule that used to be check 3 belonged to the DF3i's Press Pistol 2° — a grip with lean built in — and left with that putter on Aug 10; on a 0°-lean build, hands ahead delofts and drives it. The press was removed the same day, which also retired the old 'keep it tiny' arithmetic. The ball-forward, weight-on-the-ball question was settled on the mat back in July; what this plan adds is the number (1–2 widths inside the lead heel) and the ground reference. This plan's forgiveness section flipped twice with the bag — the mallet that muffled a wandering low point is gone, which raises the stakes and sharpens the feedback. And the reason the plan exists at all: pace decided the fate of two putters on feel alone, with zero calibrated lag sessions behind any verdict.

Aug 13: this plan was assembled from the old 'Putting Setup — Weight & Low Point' plus the posture, shaft, trail-foot and grip sections that used to live in the Routine plan — they were all one subject, and the Routine plan is now only the routine. The tape test moved to the LAG PUTTS plan. Also Aug 13: the claw came OUT of play by your call, so grip was conventional on every length. That held until Sep 10, above.

Aug 13 — a correction to this plan's own arithmetic. The 2° of effective loft quoted throughout is an ESTIMATE. No retailer and no L.A.B. page publishes a loft for the LINK.2.1, so it was inferred rather than looked up, and every de-lofting calculation downstream of it is softer than it read. The mechanism is unaffected — a forward-leaning shaft delofts a face that has little to spare, and a delofted putt skids — but the margin is not a measured quantity. Language across the plans was softened accordingly.

AUG 30 2026 — labelled the TRAIL HAND cue as Jack's own, checked against the manufacturer's design, under the new yours-versus-textbook rule. It read as handed-down instruction; it is his, and the half of it that was cut is why that distinction matters.

briefing.focus: The routine as you run it now: read it from behind, rehearse beside the ball with the pace look last, aim the FACE barely open and build the stance to it, release and RE-GRIP, and go — same beat count every putt. No forward press: this trigger changes what is IN your hands rather than where the shaft is, so the shaft is vertical at address AND at impact. How you stand and what is in your hands is the GRIP & POSTURE plan; the short ones and the lags each have their own. As of Sep 12 they are one GRIP again — the claw is out, conventional everywhere — and what differs at six feet is the stroke and a choke down the handle.
rules: READ IT FIRST — pace before break. The how lives in the Reading plan
Aim the FACE first, then build the stance to it
Set the face BARELY OPEN — that's your square
Rehearse BESIDE the ball — ball-look first, HOLE-look last, always
TRIGGER = a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP, LAST thing before the takeaway — same slot, same LIGHT pressure, and re-set into the grip you are PLAYING
Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is a pace variable
CHOKED DOWN and POP on the short ones, FULL LENGTH on the lags — conventional grip on both
Setup and grip live in GRIP & POSTURE — get low, ball inside the lead heel, shaft vertical at ADDRESS and at IMPACT
steps: Read it from BEHIND the ball — pick the line and a spot a few inches ahead of it
Step BESIDE the ball — BEND OVER, stand close, full putting posture
Rehearsal 1 — eyes on the BALL. Path and contact.
Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. This one goes last, always.
Step in — set the FACE to the spot, BARELY OPEN, then build the stance around it (trail foot a touch BACK)
Spot → ball → RE-GRIP → go. The stroke starts as a motion — quiet hands.

sections.t: THE READ — its own plan now
sections.k: What the putt is going to do, before you aim anything at it, moved to the Reading the Green plan.
sections.b:
Step one of this routine is still read it from behind — but the HOW moved out on Aug 14, the same way grip and the short stroke did.

The short version, so you are not left with nothing: behind the ball for the line, the low side for the amount, feet first on a green that looks flat, and pick the PACE before you read the break, because a putt has a different line at every speed. Past six feet the pace target is the Lag Putts circle; inside six it is seventeen inches past.

Everything else — grain, the pro side, the fall line, and the three minutes on the practice green that buy you the day's speed — is in Reading the Green.

sections.t: THE FACE — barely open is your square (your read, still unconfirmed)
sections.k: YOUR find, not the textbook's: set what reads to you as barely open — on this putter that should play as square. One check on a real green still owed; put a number on it and re-check monthly.
sections.b:
SOURCE · YOURS, AND NOT A TEXTBOOK INSTRUCTION — no putting method tells anyone to aim open. You arrived at this yourself, it is the load-bearing correction for your oldest miss, and it has not been measured on a real green. Treat it as your working setting rather than a fact.

WHAT STANDARD PRACTICE SAYS: aim the face square to the start line. That is universal, and it is not in dispute.

WHAT YOU FOUND: that setting the face to what reads to your eye as barely OPEN is what actually gets the ball started on line. Those are only in conflict if your eye and the face agree, and the whole point is that yours may not — the likely explanation is an aim error that predates every putter you have owned, so 'barely open' is the correction that cancels it and 'square' is what it produces.

SO: on this putter the face points where you set it — zero-torque means it doesn't twist through the stroke, so address IS impact, and whatever you set is what the ball gets. Set it the same way every putt and trust it until something measures it. What is NOT established is the amount: 'barely' has no number on it yet, which is the next paragraph.

Two standing guards. DON'T STACK FIXES: keep this feel, or retrain the aim picture with a mirror or a laser — never both, or the correction gets applied twice and the miss flips right. That guard got sharper on Aug 13, because a laser is a Lane B instrument by nature: watch a green line on the carpet long enough and your eye recalibrates whether you asked it to or not. Use it to MEASURE and look at the number afterwards. PUT A NUMBER ON IT: the laser does this properly now — at six feet, 1.26 inches of offset is one degree, so ten balls filmed against a marked scale turns barely open into an average you can re-check monthly. An unquantified feel drifts toward the exaggeration.

One check still owed, and it's the last one: five putts at a coin on a real green, nothing drawn on the ground, filmed from behind the ball. If the misses still fall on both sides, this closes for good. The indoor half of it can now be done any evening — the PUTTLAZR (Aug 13) reads the aim directly once it is calibrated to the FACE rather than the shaft, and the whole protocol is in Coach → At-Home Putting. Aim by feel, never at the beam.

Run the TWO-DROP TEST in the same session, since you are already in posture: drop a ball from your nose, then drop one from directly under your right eye, and measure the gap between the two marks. You are same-side dominant — right hand, right eye — and that predicts a LEFT aim bias, which is your miss exactly. The gap says whether that is live for you at all, measured bent over rather than standing up, which is the only version that counts. It is a reading, NOT a second correction: barely-open already cancels whatever aims you left, and stacking a fix on top misses right. Full write-up is in the Workshop Log.

sections.t: GRIP & POSTURE — its own plan now
sections.k: How you stand, what is in your hands, ball position, the shaft and the low point all moved to one plan.
sections.b:
Everything that is true BEFORE the putter moves now lives in GRIP & POSTURE — THE SETUP: get low and why the bend matters, the conventional grip and light pressure, ball one to two widths inside the lead heel, hands over the head of the putter, the vertical shaft at both ends, the trail foot back, lead-side pressure and the low point, and the trail hand's job on lags.

What stayed here is the ROUTINE: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger and the beat count. Those are the things you do in an order, every putt, and they are what this plan is for.

sections.t: SHORT PUTTS — they have their own plan now
sections.k: Everything inside about six feet — the choke-down, the pop stroke, the speed target and the scoreboard — lives in the Short Putts plan.
sections.b:
This plan is the stroke and the routine you run on every putt. The short ones have enough of their own content — a different grip, a different stroke shape and a different speed target — that they now have their own plan: SHORT PUTTS — THE POP STROKE.

What moved there: the pop stroke (short back, short through), the CHOKE-DOWN — which as of Sep 12 is what you do on the short ones, the claw having lasted two days — the 17-inch speed target, the loft trap that comes with rapping a ball on this face, and the 20-ball five-footer.

THE ONE THING THAT REACHES BACK INTO THIS PLAN is the trigger, and as of Sep 12 it reaches back much less far. A re-grip is the last thing you do before the stroke, and with one grip on every length it is the same physical act on every putt again. What it lands on inside six feet is a handle you are holding lower down. See THE TRIGGER below.

What stayed here, because it is true on every putt regardless of length: get low, ball position, the vertical shaft, barely open, trail foot back, the trigger, and the rehearsals.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — the release and re-grip
sections.k: Your trigger is a late release and re-grip, deliberate and in the slot as of Aug 25; it is safe on this putter because it moves PRESSURE rather than position, which is also the thing it can get wrong.
sections.b:
LIVE, your call, Aug 25: NO forward press. What you actually run is a late RELEASE AND RE-GRIP — the hands come off the handle late and re-set on it — and then you go. Which trigger you run is yours to decide.

WHY THIS IS THE SAFE KIND OF TRIGGER ON THIS PUTTER. A re-grip changes what is in your hands, not where the shaft is. Nothing leans, so nothing has to be given back, and the 2° of effective loft this head is built to deliver at zero lean stays untouched (CONFIRMED Aug 14 from L.A.B.'s own specifications). That is what lets the shaft rule go back to what it was: VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT, in this plan and in GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS. Address is a real check again, because nothing moves you off it.

THE GUARD THIS TRIGGER BRINGS WITH IT IS A DIFFERENT ONE. A press risked a POSITION; a re-grip risks a PRESSURE. Grip pressure is the main way a hand gets back into a stroke that does not want one, and re-gripping is by definition the moment you set it. So: RE-GRIP TO THE SAME LIGHT PRESSURE YOU RELEASED. If the regrab lands firmer than the grip you let go of, you have just put the trail hand back into a stroke this whole plan is built to keep it out of — and firmer hands is a quicker putt, which lands on the open fault. Nothing measures this but you, and a squeeze is one of the few things a feel reports honestly.

IT IS A DECISION NOW — your call, Aug 25, and FOR NOW is your framing and the honest one. You started from 'I kinda just do' it, which describes a habit, and a habit is the thing that goes missing exactly when you are hot or rushed, which is the moment a trigger exists for. So it is deliberate from here: the release and re-grip IS the trigger, it happens in the SAME SLOT every putt, and it is the LAST thing before the stroke starts. Provisional, held until something either measures it or you change your mind — nothing has filmed it, and none of the three triggers you have run since Aug 10 has ever been measured.

FOUR RULES for whichever trigger you run. ONE trigger, never two. SAME SLOT every putt — it is the last thing before the stroke. IT MUST SHORTEN THE DWELL — count the seconds you stand still over the ball; if a trigger hasn't shortened it, it isn't working, whatever it feels like. AND IF YOU FREEZE ANYWAY, STEP OFF — no trigger rescues a freeze you are already inside; walk back behind the ball and restart. Eight seconds, always cheaper than the putt.

AND NOW THAT IT IS A DECISION, IT CAN BE GRADED — cheaply, and this is the only trigger you have run that has ever had a number attached. A trigger has exactly one job: it gets you out of standing still. So COUNT THE DWELL. Ten putts, stopwatch or just a beat count, from your last look at the hole to the takeaway; write the average down. Do it once in the next session while the trigger is new, and again in a fortnight. If the number has not come down, the re-grip is decoration and you are running no trigger whatever it feels like. No camera, no kit, and it is the cheapest scoreboard on this plan.

AND THE LADDER IS STILL A DETECTOR, watching for something new. It used to watch for a press that leaked lean and finished putts SHORT; it now watches for a re-grip that arrives firm and sends them LONG. Either way the rule holds: if the 30-ft ladder starts showing a pattern it was not showing before, suspect the trigger before you suspect your pace.

THE CLAW WENT OUT AGAIN ON SEP 12, so the hardest version of this check lasted two days. A claw made 're-set it the same way' a DIFFERENT PHYSICAL ACT inside six feet than outside it. It is one act again on every putt — the hold your hands have spent the year learning. What remains is smaller and still worth naming: on a short putt you are re-gripping onto a handle you are holding lower down, so the slot your hand returns to is lower, not different. Re-set to your mark.

RE-GRIP INTO THE GRIP YOU ARE PLAYING, AND AT THE HEIGHT YOU ARE PLAYING IT. The release-and-re-grip is not where you decide how to hold the putter, and it is not where you decide how far down to hold it either. Both are decisions, and decisions belong behind the ball with the read rather than in the last beat before the takeaway where the trigger lives.

THE SAME-LIGHT-PRESSURE RULE STILL HOLDS, and it got easier again on Sep 12: there is a full hand on the club to report with. Light is still the instruction — L.A.B.'s own, not a preference — and a firm regrab is still the way a quiet-hands method gets undone one putt at a time.

AND THE DWELL COUNT BELOW IS NOW TWO NUMBERS, not one. Count it on a short putt and on a lag. A trigger that shortens the dwell on one grip and not the other is telling you something, and there is no reason to assume it behaves the same in both.

The full shelf of alternatives — kinetic and sensory, and what each one costs — is in the Putting Workshop Log under Aug 13; Aug 14 carries the press reversal and the Aug 25 line on it carries this one.

sections.t: THE REHEARSALS — beside the ball, pace last
sections.k: Rehearse in real posture beside the ball; ball-look first, hole-look second; same beat count every putt.
sections.b:
Read from BEHIND the ball — line, and a spot a few inches ahead of it. Then rehearse BESIDE the ball in full putting posture: same bend, same arm hang. Magnitude transfers one-to-one from that posture; behind-the-ball rehearsals read break better but run upright, so the size they teach is an approximation — and size is the thing you're training. REASONED, NOT SOURCED: that last step follows from where the arms hang in each posture. It is not a published finding and nobody has measured it on you — the ORDER below is the part that is standard teaching.

Order is fixed. Rehearsal 1, eyes on the BALL: path and contact. Rehearsal 2, eyes on the HOLE: pace. The last thing you feel is what you carry in, so the pace stroke goes last, always.

Same BEAT COUNT every putt — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts that get an extra look are the ones that come up short. Backstop worth testing: say the pace intention out loud before stepping in ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays; a word doesn't.

Past 25 feet, test eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke — as a block test on the practice green, not mid-round.

sections.t: THE STANDING WORK — where it lives
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet twice a week, and the whole protocol is in the Lag Putts plan.
sections.b:
Twice a week on the LINK, gamer ball only: 10 balls from 30 feet, logging SHORTS, SPREAD and GREEN SPEED, plus the 20/30/40 backstroke map. That is the standing work, and it belongs to pace rather than to the routine.

The full protocol, the targets and the tape test all live in the LAG PUTTS plan. The short-putt scoreboard — the 20-ball five-footer — lives in SHORT PUTTS.

sections.t: Feel versus real — how this plan is written
sections.k: Your words set the intent; the film sets the positions. Where they disagree, the film wins.
sections.b: Standing rule, in your words: the film study is king. What you're DOING — grips, triggers, decisions — is yours and authoritative. Where a POSITION or a SENSATION is claimed, the measurement outranks the description, and where there's no measurement the plan says so instead of repeating the feel as if it were established.

sections.k: History, condensed. Nothing here changes what you do above.

SEP 12 2026 — the claw is OUT after two days, your call, and you are choking down a little on the short ones instead. Nothing about the ROUTINE changed on either day: the read, the rehearsals, the aim, the trigger slot and the beat count are the same on every putt regardless of what is in your hands. What reverted is the one live check — the re-grip lands in ONE grip again on every length, at a lower point on the handle inside six feet — and the two-number dwell count the Sep 10 version introduced goes back to one.

SEP 10 2026 — the claw was the grip inside about six feet for two days, which made the re-grip trigger a different physical act on each side of the line. Reversed Sep 12, above.

Aug 25, later: the release and re-grip is a DECISION now rather than a habit you noticed — your call, and held provisionally. What that buys is a check: a trigger's one job is shortening the dwell, so the dwell count became the owed measurement and went on the trigger to-do. It is the first time a trigger in this project has had a number attached to it at all.

Aug 25: the FORWARD PRESS is out, your call — you run a late release and re-grip instead, and no press at all. Because a re-grip moves PRESSURE rather than position, the vertical-shaft rule reverted from 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' back to VERTICAL AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT across this plan, GRIP & POSTURE, SHORT PUTTS and LAG PUTTS — changed in one pass so there is one live source. The owed press clip closed with it: there is no press left to film, and the face-on clip it was folded into got easier to grade rather than harder. The guard changed shape too — it is pressure now, not position. Adopted on FEEL and UNFILMED, exactly like the two triggers before it, which is the third time in fifteen days; the Workshop Log's Aug 14 section keeps its finding and carries a SINCE UPDATED line rather than being rewritten.

Aug 14, later: the loft was confirmed at 2° from L.A.B.'s specifications, so the trigger section no longer calls it an estimate. Nothing about the press changed — a confirmed-small loft budget makes the case for a press that RECOVERS slightly stronger, not weaker.

Aug 14: the FORWARD PRESS came back, your call — you tried the shelf and it felt best of them all. It replaces the trail-thumb press, which was only ever yours by decision too and was never filmed. The Aug 10 'NO FORWARD PRESS' rule and this plan's own 'forward press stays out permanently' line are both gone; the vertical-shaft rule was re-scoped from 'address AND impact' to 'IMPACT, and the press recovers into it' across the Routine, GRIP & POSTURE and SHORT PUTTS plans, so there is only one live source. Aug 10: the press came out (your call — the 2° loft budget has nothing to spare, and a varying press is a varying pace). The DF3i was returned for distance control; its Press Pistol 2° went with it, and every 'hands even / hands ahead' cue died with that grip. The claw reopened for shorts — the old 'claw shelved' verdict came from a different putter, a different grip and a live left miss, so it doesn't bind. 'Hands over the ball' was corrected to 'hands over the HEAD of the putter' — the corrected version matches the Jul 30 stills exactly (vertical shaft = hands ~1.35" behind the ball centre), the first time a feel and a measurement have landed on each other in this project.

Aug 10 pm film: three putts on a lined mat went 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — the one-way LEFT pull from Jul 30 (1.5°, 1.7°) did not reproduce. Jul 30 film, still standing: SBST path confirmed across four putters; tempo 2.0:1; early lift closed; stance line closed (toes never open); vertical shaft repeatable to 0.3°. Pace remains the open fault — it decided the fate of two putters without ever being measured, which is why the ladder is the standing work.

Aug 13 — two workshops, both written up in full in the PUTTING WORKSHOP LOG rather than here. THE TRAIL HAND: the L.A.B. framing checked out, 'let the head release' did not and was cut, and the lead-hand half was scoped to the lags because the claw inverts it. THE TRIGGER: the trail thumb press is yours by decision, and the old 'NO PRESS' rule was renamed NO FORWARD PRESS to kill the collision. Neither has been filmed — that the thumb press leaves the shaft alone is reasoning from where your thumb sits, not a measurement.

Aug 13, later: the setup and grip sections moved out to GRIP & POSTURE and the claw section moved to SHORT PUTTS, leaving this plan as the routine alone. Also Aug 13 — the claw came out of play by your call; conventional on every length now, with the claw held as the reserve.

sections.t: The ladder — this is the grind
sections.k: Ten balls from thirty feet, twice a week, three numbers written down.
sections.b:
Ten balls, 30 feet, on the LINK. Twice a week. Log three things every time:

SHORTS — how many of the ten finish short of the hole. Target: no more than 1 in 10. A putt that finishes short had a zero per cent chance.

SPREAD — front-to-back distance between the nearest and furthest stopping points. This is the actual measurement of distance control and the number that shows improvement. Target: inside 6 feet.

GREEN SPEED — estimated stimp, or name the surface honestly (that mat, this practice green). Not optional: a stroke that finishes perfectly on an 8–9 runs four to six feet past from 30 feet on an 11, so build the curve on at least TWO speeds before trusting it.

Then the calibration set, five minutes: 20, 30 and 40 feet, three balls each, noting where the BACKSTROKE ENDS for each distance — a landmark you can repeat. Written down, that mapping is the curve.

sections.t: Where distance comes from
sections.k: Stroke length at a fixed tempo — if tempo moves with distance, the curve never stabilises.
sections.b:
The ingredient most people are missing, you have: tempo measured 2.0:1 on this head against a 2:1 target. So the discipline in every ladder session is: same tempo, always — count it, hum it, whatever keeps it stable — and change the LENGTH.

The failure mode is the reverse: keeping the backstroke roughly constant and varying how hard you hit it. That works at one distance and falls apart everywhere else. If you catch yourself hitting AT a long one, that rep is the fault showing itself — note it on the sheet.

Once three distances have a repeatable backstroke landmark, everything between them is interpolation, and lag putting becomes a reference you consult instead of a feeling you summon.

sections.t: Strike — the hidden speed leak
sections.k: Off-centre contact bleeds ball speed. Twelve minutes of foot powder before any verdict on this putter.
sections.b:
A putt struck off the middle loses ball speed, so the same stroke finishes shorter — and inconsistently, because the miss moves. A heel strike also rotates the face closed. One cause, both faults, and it has never been measured on any putter you've owned.

This blade raises the stakes: less MOI than a mallet, so the same miss costs more speed and more face angle — and its riser hosel makes the true centre impossible to find by eye. If strike is your leak, the ladder will show it as a wide spread, and the tape test will show you where it's coming from.

So run the tape test EARLY — tap test for the true sweet spot, then foot-powder sheets from 5 and 30 feet, with the 30-footer as the verdict. The full protocol is the next section. Use the barely-open address, since that's the setup you actually play.

sections.t: The tape test — the whole protocol, twelve minutes
sections.k: Hang it and tap it to find the true sweet spot, then two powder sheets at two distances — the 30-footer is the verdict.
sections.b:
STEP ONE — FIND THE TRUE SWEET SPOT. Hang the putter from the top of the grip so it swings free. Tap the face heel-to-toe with a pencil eraser and watch the head: everywhere off-centre it TWISTS, and at one spot it swings straight back with no twist. That spot is the true sweet spot. Mark it with a sliver of tape.

Then check the mark against the sight line. On this head the shaft is a poor pointer to where the mass sits — the riser hosel offsets it — so don't trust your eye. If the mark and the sight line disagree, that disagreement is a finding on its own: you have been lining up a spot that isn't the middle.

STEP TWO — THE POWDER SHEETS. Coat the face with foot-powder spray. Hit 10 putts from 5 feet. Photograph the face. Re-coat, hit 10 from 30 feet, photograph again. Don't wipe between putts — the overlapping marks ARE the data. Use the setup you actually play: conventional grip on all of them as of Sep 12, FULL LENGTH on the 30-footers and CHOKED DOWN on the 5-footers, with a barely-open face and hands over the head throughout. THE THIRD COAT IS WORTH KEEPING even though the grip no longer differs — run 10 more at 5 feet at FULL LENGTH, kept separate, because that pair is the only thing that can say what the choke does to your strike at a distance where everything else is held constant. That is a smaller question than the one this third coat was added for on Sep 10, and it is a cleaner one.

HOW TO READ THEM. TIGHT CLUSTER ON THE MARK — strike isn't your leak, and pace work is pure stroke-length calibration. CLUSTER OFF-CENTRE, especially toward the HEEL — one cause explaining both open faults at once, since heel contact rotates the face closed (starts it left) and bleeds ball speed (finishes short); fixable with distance-to-ball and eyeline, not with a new putter. BROAD SCATTER — the ladder's spread has its cause, because a strike that moves is a ball speed that moves.

The 30-FOOT sheet is the one that matters — long putts are where a speed leak shows. The 5-foot sheet is the baseline that says whether the leak is stroke-length dependent. Send both photos when you run it.

sections.t: Setup for pace — four lines
sections.k: Marked ball position, vertical shaft, quiet hands, gamer ball. Pace has no other setup inputs.
sections.b:
BALL marked 1–2 ball-widths inside the lead heel, same spot every rep — launch is sensitive to it, and a wandering ball position reads as bad distance control even when the stroke was fine.

HANDS OVER THE HEAD OF THE PUTTER, shaft vertical AT ADDRESS AND AT IMPACT — and as of Aug 25 there is nothing in front of it: the forward press is out and your trigger is a RE-GRIP, which is a pressure change rather than a position change, so it does not touch this. That is the best outcome this plan could have asked for. A lag is nothing but pace, a varying launch is a varying pace, and with nothing leaning the shaft there is nothing to vary. What DOES carry to this plan is the re-grip's own guard: land it on the same light pressure every time, because firmer hands is a quicker putt and this is the plan that pace is measured on. Its rules live in the Routine plan.

QUIET HANDS, shoulders run it.

GAMER BALL ONLY on all pace work, and CONVENTIONAL grip — which as of Sep 12 is the grip on every length again. The comparability claim that was removed on Sep 10 comes most of the way back, and it is worth stating precisely rather than simply restoring it: the ladder numbers and the short-putt numbers are made with the SAME HOLD again, so a difference between them can no longer be a grip. They still differ by stroke length and now by a CHOKE on the short side, so they are readable side by side rather than as one series. Nothing about this plan's own numbers has ever changed through any of it — the ladder has always been conventional at full length and still is.

AND THE TRAIL-HAND FEEL CUE IS STILL EXCLUSIVELY YOURS OUT HERE, for the reason it always was rather than the one it briefly had. The right hand sensing the weight of the head is a distance cue, and there is no distance to feel inside six feet. For two days it was ALSO impossible in there, because a claw has no feel hand; that guard went out with the claw on Sep 12 and the original reason stands on its own. It is a lag cue. Do not carry it in. What must also NOT come out here is the pop stroke: a short backstroke with force added is the exact failure this plan exists to prevent.

sections.t: What the numbers are for now
sections.k: The putter is settled, so the ladder stopped being a trial and became a calibration.
sections.b:
The keep-or-return gate this section used to hold is CLOSED — you kept the LINK by decision on Aug 12 and shut the return window yourself. That changes what the numbers are for, and it is a better job than the one they had.

They are no longer evidence in a trial. Nothing on the ladder can now send a head back, which means nothing on the ladder needs defending. Two weeks of numbers at two different green speeds plus the tape test now buy you a power curve you can consult instead of a feeling you summon — and if the spread stays wide with a centred sheet, the answer is head WEIGHT or reps, not a fifth putter.

Head weight is the dial, and it is the cheapest one left. A heavier head produces a shorter, more repeatable stroke for a given distance, which usually helps lag control; a lighter head asks for a longer stroke and gives more feel on the short ones. Don't touch it before you have baseline numbers, or you will be changing two things at once and learn nothing.

And the standing rule survives everything: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

sections.t: What's already settled
sections.k: Path, tempo, lift, stance — measured, closed, and none of them walked out with any putter.
sections.b:
Path: straight, SBST, confirmed across four heads. Tempo: 2.0:1 on this putter. Early lift: closed on film. Stance line: square, never open. Start line: downgraded — the one-way left pull did not reproduce across three measured putts.

What's open is pace and strike, and both are the same twelve minutes and the same ladder away from having numbers. The rule stands: the next thing that changes should be a NUMBER on the card, not a head in the bag.

SEP 12 2026 — the claw is OUT after two days, your call, and the short ones are played CHOKED DOWN on a conventional grip instead. Out here nothing changes at all: full length on the handle, conventional, as it has been all year. Two things revert. The grip line stops being a two-grip instruction and becomes a handle instruction. And the comparability claim comes most of the way back — same hold on both sides again, so a difference between the ladder and the short putts cannot be a grip, though a choke and a stroke length still separate them.

SEP 10 2026 — the claw was the grip inside about six feet for two days, which briefly made this plan's grip line a real split and removed the claim that the two sets of numbers were comparable. Reversed Sep 12, above. The tape test's third coat was added then and survives with a smaller job.

Aug 25: the forward press came out by your decision, replaced by a late release and re-grip, so this plan's 'SAME SIZE every time' guard on the press retires — there is no press to keep the same size. The reasoning behind it does not retire and never has: a varying launch is a varying pace. It now applies to grip PRESSURE instead of shaft position, which is the one thing a re-grip can vary.

Aug 14: the forward press came back as the trigger by your call, so this plan's 'no FORWARD press' rule is retired and re-scoped like the others — vertical AT IMPACT, with the press recovering into it. The reasoning that rule carried is NOT retired and is now the guard on the press itself: a varying launch is a varying pace, and pace is the open fault on this plan.

The DF3i went back on Aug 10 for distance control — after being benched for pace Jul 30, reprieved Aug 1 and returned Aug 10: three verdicts in eleven days, all on feel, zero calibrated lag sessions. That pattern, not the putter, is what this plan exists to break. The Aug 1 'pace felt dialled' round was a scramble on 8–9 stimp greens — the friendliest read available. The Aug 10 outdoor session scored ~20 putts off above-ground cups: nine dead, worst ~4 ft, nothing long — first real evidence pace is closer than the returns implied. The blue ball scattered 1.2–1.5 ft on putts the white killed from the same spot — hence the gamer-ball rule. Both reds on the evolution grid (face at impact, start line) were measured on this head Jul 30; the start-line red was downgraded Aug 10 pm after the mat set came back 0.8° right / 1.0° left / 0.6° right — dispersion, no bias.

Aug 13: the Tape Test folded in from its own plan — it was always the same subject as this one, since strike is a distance fault before it is a line fault. Written Aug 2 for the DF3i, moved to the LINK Aug 10, still unrun on any of the four putters owned this month. Two Aug 10 pointers both aim at it: the evening mat putts scattered ~0.8° either side with no bias (a moving strike is the leading explanation on a head that cannot twist), and the blue ball spread 1.2-1.5 ft on putts the white killed. The keep-or-return gate closed Aug 12 when you kept the putter by decision.

sections.t: Sep 12 2026 — The claw is out after two days, and what the choke-down costs instead
sections.k: Your call closes the grip question and the claw never produced a number, so nothing had to be unwound — but the choke that replaces it is a pace change with no number on it, and pace is the open fault.
sections.b:
THE QUESTION. On Sep 10 the claw became the grip inside about six feet, by your decision. On Sep 12 you reversed it: 'always the claw is out, hated it. Just kinda choking up a little on the short ones. 32 putts today so it was good.' Both calls are about what you DO, so both are authoritative and neither was waiting on a number. What this section works out is what the reversal actually costs and buys, and what the choke-down leaves unmeasured.

WHAT CHECKED OUT — and it is a real verdict, not a polite one. SOURCE · STANDARD PRACTICE. Gripping down the handle on short putts is ordinary, widely taught and common on tour. It shortens the lever, so the same hand movement makes a smaller stroke and less ball speed; it brings the hands closer to the ball; and it takes shaft out from under the hands, so the head feels lighter and a hand that wants to hit at it has less to hit with.
